sights.name: Palazzo del Lavoro
sights.blurb: A giant square hall roofed by 16 freestanding concrete "mushroom" columns with steel umbrella caps. The glass and metal façades are rusting and broken. It is the southern gateway to the city.
sights.when: Owned by CDP Immobiliare since 2020. Safety works were completed in early 2025. A shopping-centre plan was dropped. A rumoured Qatari cultural investment (Al Mayassa Al-Thani, ~€500M) reached "stallo" by April 2026.
sights.q: Palazzo del Lavoro, Via Ventimiglia 211, Torino

sights.name: Torino Esposizioni
sights.blurb: Nervi's 1948–50 prefabricated ferrocement vault, the "cattedrale moderna", plus Morandi's 1959 underground hall. It has been restored by Rafael Moneo with Isolarchitetti.
sights.when: Opening date repeatedly slipped (30 June 2026, then "autumn"). Presenting "Vale", the new Valentino cultural hub, Mayor Lo Russo announced 11 December 2026 as the public opening, with programming starting in November (Exibart). Not open on 20 Oct 2026.
sights.q: Torino Esposizioni, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 15, Torino

sights.name: Lingotto: Pista 500 rooftop track
sights.blurb: The 1920s Fiat factory's rooftop banked test track, 28 m up. It is now a planted art garden (about 6,000 m², about 40,000 plants), with Renzo Piano's "Bolla" and "Scrigno" additions.
sights.when: Pinacoteca Agnelli is open Tue–Sun 10:00–19:00 (schedule valid 21 Sept–28 Oct 2026). Per Turismo Torino (the official tourist board), the Pinacoteca + Pista 500 combo costs €12 full / €8 reduced, and the Pista 500 alone €4 full / €2 reduced.

sights.name: Santo Volto and Parco Dora
sights.blurb: A seven-tower brick church on a former Fiat Ferriere steelworks site. The roughly 60 m steelworks chimney is kept as a "campanile" wrapped in a steel helix with a cross on top, and the bells actually sit at its base.
sights.when: Active parish, free, open around services. The park is public.
sights.q: Chiesa del Santo Volto, Via Val della Torre 11, Torino

sights.name: Cimitero Parco
sights.blurb: About 690,000 m² of rolling lawns. Artificial hillocks hide the concrete burial complexes, and simple slabs lie flush in the grass with the Alps behind.
sights.when: Municipal cemetery, free. Check opening hours on the comune site.

sights.name: Piazza Risorgimento air-raid shelter
sights.blurb: Three parallel reinforced-concrete galleries about 40 m long and 4.5 m wide, 12 m underground, with 80 cm walls. Wartime rules of conduct are still painted on the walls. The access turrets have murals by XEL.
sights.when: Only on special openings. These include Museo Diffuso della Resistenza tours, FAI days and Monumenti Aperti (one edition ran Sat–Sun 10–12 and 14:30–16). Book through the Museo Diffuso (011 01120780).

sights.name: Corso Taranto IACP housing
sights.blurb: Sixteen eight-storey heavy-prefab slabs (652 flats) lined up on the heliothermic axis, designed by Nello Renacco. These are Turin's nearest analogue to a Falowiec or Aillaud estate in spirit, though not in scale.

sights.name: Chiesa del Gesù Redentore
sights.blurb: Bare brick walls under a faceted exposed reinforced-concrete vault, with a single nave.
sights.when: Active parish. The roof was restored in 2002.
sights.q: Chiesa Gesù Redentore, Piazza Giovanni XXIII 26, Torino

sights.name: Torre BBPR (Reale Mutua tower)
sights.blurb: A brick-clad "post-rationalist/brutalist" tower with oriel bays and porticoes, Milan-school neo-liberty. It is Turin's cousin of the Torre Velasca.

sights.name: Nietzsche's last lodging
sights.blurb: A marble plaque on the façade. His room was the fifth window from the corner, on the 4th floor, above the Galleria Subalpina entrance.
sights.when: Street plaque, always visible. The flat is private.

sights.name: Palazzo Campana
sights.blurb: A grand palazzo with a university entrance.
sights.when: University building. The courtyard is usually accessible in term time.
sights.q: Palazzo Campana, Via Carlo Alberto 10, Torino

sights.name: Cannonballs embedded in façades
sights.blurb: Iron shot from the 1706 siege and the 1799 fighting, walled into façades as memorials: two in the Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana courtyard (Via della Consolata 1 bis), more on Piazza San Carlo, Piazza Palazzo di Città and the Consolata.
sights.when: Public façades. Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana's courtyard is reachable during business hours.

sights.name: Fetta di Polenta
sights.blurb: A many-storey wedge-shaped house whose narrow end is 54 cm wide. Built by the Mole's architect.
sights.when: Private building, view from the street.
sights.q: Casa Scaccabarozzi, Via Giulia di Barolo 9, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Mulassano
sights.blurb: A 31 m² Liberty-style café, a Locale Storico d'Italia since 1985. Inside, a plaque reads "Nel 1926, la signora Angela Demichelis Nebiolo, inventò il tramezzino". The name is attributed to D'Annunzio, and sources give 1925 or 1926.
sights.when: Open, roughly 09:30–20:00 (to 19:30 Tue/Wed per TripAdvisor). It is classed as B (a "first"), not C.

sights.name: Palazzo Carignano
sights.blurb: Guarini's undulating brick baroque façade.
sights.q: Palazzo Carignano, Via Accademia delle Scienze 5, Torino

sights.name: Piazza San Carlo 2017 plaque
sights.blurb: A plaque placed in 2019 for the victims of the panic during the Juventus Champions League final screening, which was triggered by a robbery gang using pepper spray. Three people eventually died.

sights.name: "Baci Urbani"
sights.blurb: An oversized metal "piercing" ring stuck into the corner of an 18th-century building. It was meant as a temporary art installation and never removed.

sights.name: Ristorante Del Cambio
sights.blurb: Regional tourism site Piemonteitalia: "Nella sala più ampia è conservato il tavolo dove sedeva abitualmente il Conte Camillo Benso di Cavour". Rolling Stone Italia: "Il suo tavolo è ancora segnato con una targa commemorativa".
sights.when: Open, Michelin one star. Dinner roughly 19:30–23:30, Sunday lunch, plus a bistro at lunch. You can ask for Cavour's table when booking. Expensive; check delcambio.it.
sights.q: Ristorante Del Cambio, Piazza Carignano 2, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Elena
sights.blurb: Comune di Torino: "oggi si può fare colazione dove Cesare Pavese trascorreva il proprio tempo a scrivere". The original red breccia-marble tables survive. Giuseppe Carpano is said to have perfected his vermouth here in 1889–1902.
sights.when: Open. Mon–Fri 08–00, closed Wednesday; Sat 09–01; Sun 09–00 (official site).
sights.q: Caffè Elena, Piazza Vittorio Veneto 5, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Fiorio
sights.blurb: Frequented by Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo, Santorre di Santarosa and Cavour, who is said to have founded the Whist Club here.
sights.when: No closure reported. Check hours. Ignore one guide's wrong address (Piazza Castello 29).

sights.name: Al Bicerin
sights.blurb: By long tradition, Cavour drank here while waiting for the royal family to leave the Consolata sanctuary; one source frames it as "legend has it". Names on the wall (Dumas, Puccini, Nietzsche, Gozzano, Calvino) are tradition.
sights.when: Open, closed Wednesdays. About 08:30–19:30 (sources vary). Tiny, so expect a queue.
sights.q: Al Bicerin, Piazza della Consolata 5, Torino

sights.name: Caffè San Carlo
sights.blurb: A Risorgimento patriots' café (D'Azeglio, Cavour, Rattazzi, Giolitti, Crispi), closed several times for suspected subversion. A 1920s literary circle met here.
sights.when: Open, roughly 08:00–00:00. Management has changed several times, and it was closed for restoration 1953–63.
sights.q: Caffè San Carlo, Piazza San Carlo 156, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Platti
sights.blurb: Popular sources: Luigi Einaudi, Cesare Pavese, Natalia Ginzburg, and the founders of Fiat and Lavazza.
sights.when: Changed owner in Sept 2026. Gerla 1927 sold it to Villa Cimena Luxury Events (Balma family) through a new company, Platti il Salotto del Gusto S.r.l. Closed from about 1 Oct 2026 for restyling.
sights.q: Caffè Platti, Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 72, Torino

sights.name: Biblioteca Reale (Royal Library)
sights.when: Tourists see the Salone with a Musei Reali ticket, Mon and Fri 9:00–13:30 and Tue, Thu and Sat 13:30–18:30; currently it also hosts "Margherita, prima Regina d'Italia" until 6 Jan 2027.

sights.name: Accademia delle Scienze library
sights.blurb: Lagrange was a founder. Early members included Monge, Laplace, d'Alembert and Euler. It holds Coronelli globes.
sights.when: "Esclusivamente su appuntamento", Mon–Thu 9–13 and 15–17, Fri 9–13, through a form. Casual visitors usually get in only during events or conferences.
sights.q: Accademia delle Scienze, Via Maria Vittoria 3, Torino

sights.name: Teatro Regio (Mollino)
sights.blurb: Mollino's brick-and-concrete shell (1967–73) inside Juvarra's surviving façade: foyers, the oval hall, and backstage workshops on the tour.
sights.when: 'Il Regio dietro le quinte' tours: Sat 15:00 and 16:30, Sun 11:00, 1 h, €10, Italian only, max 25. Tickets online from the Monday before each month's first tour.

sights.name: Palazzo degli Affari (Mollino)
sights.blurb: Chamber of Commerce block raised on a central core, a four-storey 'blade' linked by an aerial walkway, and Mollino's helical stair (1964–73).
sights.when: Working public offices; walk into the lobby in office hours. Occasional paid tours (Fondazione per l'architettura).
sights.q: Camera di Commercio, Via San Francesco da Paola 24, Torino

sights.name: Ex Borsa Valori
sights.blurb: Gabetti, Isola and Raineri's 1952–56 trading hall with its vaulted concrete roof, facing Piazzale Valdo Fusi. Closed since trading ended in 1992.
sights.when: Exterior only. Conversion planned: works may start 2028, finish 2030.
sights.q: Ex Borsa Valori, Via San Francesco da Paola 28, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Nuovo (university)
sights.blurb: The hulking 1960s humanities slab on an exposed steel frame: Turin's 1968-era campus monolith.
sights.when: Open in university hours; expect closures during protests (occupied 28 Jan–2 Feb 2026).

sights.name: Casa dell'Obelisco (Jaretti & Luzi)
sights.blurb: Undulating, banded 'litocemento' façades and an oyster-shaped entrance (1954–59): the provocative icon of Turin Neoliberty.

sights.name: Torri Pitagora (Jaretti & Luzi)
sights.blurb: Two ten-storey towers hollowed at the base into a 'forest of pillars', growing heavier as they rise (1962–68).
sights.when: Private, exterior only; Open House has offered interior visits.

sights.name: Falchera (Astengo's INA-Casa village)
sights.blurb: Turin's first INA-Casa satellite (1951–60): red-brick blocks on a hexagonal grid around a civic centre with a mushroom column. Falchera Nuova's 1970s towers stand just north.
sights.when: Public streets. Fondazione per l'architettura runs occasional guided walks.

sights.name: Le Vallette estate
sights.blurb: 71 ha of 1958–68 public housing by 45 architects (Gabetti & Isola, Levi Montalcini and others): towers, slabs and 'Scandinavian' courts. Gabetti & Isola's school is at Via dei Mughetti 26.
sights.when: Public streets; local history centre runs Open House tours.
sights.q: Piazza Eugenio Montale, Le Vallette, Torino

sights.name: San Paolo Apostolo
sights.blurb: Mario Bianco's all-concrete central plan (1967–69): a complex roof on massive pillars that seems to float above a ribbon of glass.
sights.when: Active parish; go around Mass times.
sights.q: Chiesa San Paolo Apostolo, Via Michele Berrino 12, Torino

sights.name: Santa Teresa di Gesù Bambino
sights.blurb: Post-conciliar church whose bell tower and roof dominate the local skyline (1961–70); OAT 2010 award.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Teresa di Gesù Bambino, Via Giovanni da Verrazzano 48, Torino

sights.name: Gesù Operaio
sights.blurb: Felice Bardelli's 1963–67 church (he co-designed Palazzo Nuovo), with a gym in the undercroft; the census flags its structural system.
sights.when: Active parish. Exposed concrete unconfirmed; check in person.
sights.q: Chiesa Gesù Operaio, Via Leoncavallo 18, Torino

sights.name: San Luca Evangelista
sights.blurb: Roggero's 1967–71 church among the Mirafiori Sud public housing; also a MITO concert venue.
sights.when: Mass Sat 18:15, Sun 9:30/11/18:15. Exposed concrete unconfirmed.
sights.q: Chiesa San Luca Evangelista, Via Celeste Negarville 14, Torino

sights.name: San Michele Arcangelo
sights.blurb: Dolci and Tripodi's 1967–70 church with a pointed 'cuspide' roof, a short walk from Falchera.
sights.q: Chiesa San Michele Arcangelo, Corso Vercelli 390, Torino

sights.name: San Francesco di Sales
sights.blurb: Mario Bianco's 1973–78 church, by the designer of San Paolo Apostolo.
sights.when: Active parish. Materials and pin unverified.
sights.q: Chiesa San Francesco di Sales, Via Malta 42, Torino

sights.name: Santa Maria Goretti
sights.blurb: Modest 1964–67 church by Carbonara and Berardo in Parella.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Maria Goretti, Via Vittorio Actis 20, Torino

sights.name: Italia '61 monorail stumps
sights.blurb: 14 of the 58 spans of the 1961 Alweg monorail viaduct on inverted-pyramid concrete piers, plus the south station shell, by the lake.
sights.when: Public park, always visible. Graffiti, spalling concrete, rough sleepers.
sights.q: Parco Italia 61, Corso Unità d'Italia, Torino

sights.name: Italia '61 illuminated fountain
sights.blurb: The original 1961 illuminated fountain near the Palavela, 'still there, though left to itself'.

sights.name: Monorail north station (Casa UGI)
sights.blurb: The 1961 north station, now a home for families of children with cancer.
sights.when: In use; exterior only, be discreet.
sights.q: Casa UGI, Corso Unità d'Italia 70, Torino

sights.name: Olympic arch and footbridge
sights.blurb: The 69 m red arch and the cable-stayed footbridge over the railway (2003–05), from the 1932 market arcades to the coloured athletes' village.
sights.when: Footbridge public; parts of ex-MOI vacant or fenced.
sights.q: Passerella Olimpica, Via Giordano Bruno, Torino

sights.name: Trincerone (sunken rail corridor)
sights.blurb: A 5.5 km sunken ex-rail corridor, overgrown and dumped in, seen from bridges and street edges.
sights.when: Time-sensitive: Metro 2 works start in the first half of 2027. View from public streets only.

sights.name: OSI-Ghia ruins
sights.blurb: A 1960 coachbuilding plant, abandoned since 2001.
sights.when: Fenced, exterior only; local press advises avoiding the area.

sights.name: ThyssenKrupp steelworks
sights.blurb: Vast vacant sheds of the steelworks where seven workers died in the December 2007 fire.
sights.when: Fenced, exterior only. Visit with respect.

sights.name: Ex-Superga factory
sights.blurb: Sheds of the plant where the canvas sneaker was made, abandoned since 1998.
sights.when: Exterior only; becoming a Paratissima culture hub (about three years of works).

sights.name: Officine Grandi Motori
sights.blurb: Fiat's 1911 'Basilica' hall and the 'Lingottino', shells on a fenced demolition and clean-up site.
sights.when: Time-sensitive: works since Feb 2025; view from Corso Vigevano.
sights.q: Officine Grandi Motori, Corso Vigevano, Torino

sights.name: Le Nuove prison shelter
sights.blurb: An air-raid shelter 18 m deep inside the 19th-century prison, told through political and Jewish prisoners' testimony.
sights.when: Guided only, booking required (011 7604881): 25 places, about 1 h 15, €8 / €5, Abbonamento Musei valid.
sights.q: Museo del Carcere Le Nuove, Via Paolo Borsellino 3, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Civico air-raid shelter
sights.blurb: A 1940 shelter 10 m under the town hall's courtyard: 20 × 3 m for 50 staff, rusting gas-tight doors and original wall signs.
sights.when: Free visits since 2017; current schedule not found.
sights.q: Palazzo Civico, Piazza Palazzo di Città 1, Torino

sights.name: Mirafiori shelter and Chiesa della Visitazione
sights.blurb: A 1934 concrete church with crypt, and the shelter that protected the Mirafiori borgo, on a 90-minute tour from the lost Savoy castle site.
sights.when: No tour dates bookable now; watch arteemusei.com.
sights.q: Chiesa della Visitazione, Strada Castello di Mirafiori 42, Torino

sights.name: PalaRuffini (Vitellozzi)
sights.blurb: Vitellozzi's 1959–61 concrete arena for Italia '61, twin of his Rome Palazzetto; his own favourite.
sights.when: Exterior always visible in Parco Ruffini; inside on match days (Basket Torino).

sights.name: Fiat Mirafiori: Palazzina and Corso Tazzoli
sights.blurb: The 220 m white-stone office block (1937–39) and a clinker front almost 1 km long on Corso Tazzoli; Porta 5 was the gate of the 1970s labour struggles.
sights.when: Private; view from the pavements. The Palazzina reopens as a campus by 2027, so expect works.

sights.name: Tempio Crematorio and Luogo del Ricordo
sights.blurb: Italy's second crematorium (1882) with Cordero sculptures in its modern garden, and the city's ash-scattering garden of three fountains over Luserna stone.

sights.name: Palazzo di Giustizia
sights.blurb: A 300 m courthouse (1990–2000) in brick and 30,000 m² of glass: megastructure scale, not concrete.
sights.q: Palazzo di Giustizia, Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 130, Torino

sights.name: Santi Apostoli, Piossasco
sights.blurb: Gabetti & Isola's church built from prefab factory-shed parts (1969–73): 24 m concrete trusses, U-glass walls, a giant precast cross. Built for Fiat Rivalta workers.
sights.when: Active parish, open around Mass. Car or bus; pair with Collegno.
sights.q: Chiesa Santi Apostoli, Via Pinerolo 161, Piossasco

sights.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, Moriondo
sights.blurb: Nicola Mosso's pentagonal church: six exposed pillars, a roof broken into triangles, light through the gaps. A sibling of the Redentore.
sights.q: Chiesa San Pietro in Vincoli, Via Duca d'Aosta 3, Moncalieri

sights.name: SS. Trinità, Nichelino
sights.blurb: Pratesi's 1970–73 church: exposed concrete beams knitting into a net, modelled on the Redentore. Roof leaks and decaying concrete.
sights.when: Active parish (Via Stupinigi 16); check the pin.
sights.q: Parrocchia SS. Trinità, Via Stupinigi 16, Nichelino

sights.name: FATA HQ, Pianezza (Niemeyer + Morandi)
sights.blurb: Niemeyer and Morandi's 1976–79 'land bridge': a 100 m office block hung from great arches, with 21.30 m cantilevers on six hollow piers.
sights.when: Company offices; photograph from the road, don't enter the grounds.

sights.name: Collegno: Certosa and ex-asylum
sights.blurb: A 17th-century charterhouse that became the Royal asylum in 1852; walls down after 1978, now a park of 40 ha with some abandoned pavilions.
sights.when: Park open daily; free visits with the Ciceroni Collegnesi. Pavilions not visitable.
sights.q: Certosa Reale, Via Martiri XXX Aprile 30, Collegno

sights.name: Casa Martini, Pessione
sights.blurb: The wine museum in the 18th-century cellars of the first Martini & Rossi plant (1864), with stills and presses.
sights.q: Casa Martini, Piazza Luigi Rossi 2, Pessione

sights.name: 1864 bullet dent, Caval ëd Bronz
sights.blurb: A bullet dent on the Cateau-Cambrésis bas-relief of the equestrian statue, from the night of 22 September 1864.
sights.when: Always visible; look at the plinth reliefs.
sights.q: Monumento a Emanuele Filiberto, Piazza San Carlo, Torino

sights.name: Rondò della Forca: Cafasso monument
sights.blurb: A 1960 bronze of the 'gallows priest' Cafasso, on the spot where public hangings were held 1835–1853.
sights.q: Rondò della Forca, Corso Regina Margherita, Torino

sights.name: Piazza Carlina: guillotine square
sights.blurb: No marker: under French rule (1798–1814) the guillotine stood about where Cavour's statue is; 423 executions reported. Gramsci's 1919–21 lodging plaque is at no. 15.

sights.name: Sacrario del Martinetto
sights.blurb: The small rifle range where RSI firing squads shot about sixty partisans in 1943–45; a stone post and a plaque with 59 names.
sights.when: Memorial site; check access times with the Museo Diffuso.
sights.q: Sacrario del Martinetto, Corso Svizzera, Torino

sights.name: Pian del Lot memorial
sights.blurb: Granite monument where 27 prisoners from Le Nuove were shot on 2 April 1944; the first municipal plaque on the back still shows doubt about some names.
sights.when: Outdoor, always open; car or bus up the Maddalena road.
sights.q: Sacrario Pian del Lot, Strada Comunale di Pian del Lot, Torino

sights.name: Via Cibrario 1: 'in questo luogo'
sights.blurb: The plaque on the exact spot where nine partisans, two of them unknown Frenchmen, were shot on 12 October 1944. Another for nine shot stands on Piazza Statuto.

sights.name: Piazza XVIII Dicembre plaque (1922)
sights.blurb: Plaque for the 18–20 December 1922 Fascist massacre: 11 killed by Brandimarte's squads, the Camera del Lavoro burned. A second plaque is in the metro station.

sights.name: Angelo Azzurro plaque (1977)
sights.blurb: Where Roberto Crescenzio, 22, died after militants firebombed the bar on 1 October 1977 believing it a neo-fascist haunt. Plaque 2017.
sights.when: Street plaque; the premises are a bar again.

sights.name: Corso Re Umberto 54: Casalegno
sights.blurb: The doorway where the Red Brigades shot La Stampa's deputy editor Carlo Casalegno on 16 November 1977; nothing on the street recalls it.

sights.name: Pietro Micca museum and siege tunnels
sights.blurb: Down to 6 and 14 m into the 1706 counter-mine galleries, to the stair Pietro Micca ran down and the spot where his body was found.
sights.when: Tue–Sun 10–18; tunnel visits booked (011 01167580) at 10:30, 14:30, 16:30 (+15:30 Sun). Abbonamento Musei valid.
sights.q: Museo Pietro Micca, Via Guicciardini 7, Torino

sights.name: Mastio della Cittadella
sights.blurb: The surviving keep of the 1564 citadel, now the Artillery museum. Its front 'door' is a fake, topped by a grimacing mask to mock invaders.
sights.when: Opens for exhibitions; hours irregular. Exterior always visible.
sights.q: Mastio della Cittadella, Corso Galileo Ferraris 2, Torino

sights.name: Teatro di Torino ruin
sights.blurb: Perimeter walls and part of the foyer of the 1857 theatre gutted by bombs on 8 December 1942: 'the only conspicuous visible memory' of the war damage.
sights.when: Visible from the street, no entry.

sights.name: Piazza Valdo Fusi: the bombing void
sights.blurb: An open square over a car park where a whole city block, the old Politecnico, stood before the bombs.

sights.name: Synagogue and the walled-up door
sights.blurb: The Moorish-style synagogue, gutted in the 21 November 1942 raid with only its four towers standing; on Via Sant'Anselmo the old 'brides' door' at no. 7 is bricked up.
sights.when: Exterior always; interior by booking with the Jewish Community.
sights.q: Sinagoga, Via San Pio V 12, Torino

sights.name: Monte dei Cappuccini shelter mouths
sights.blurb: Eight WWII tunnel entrances in the hillside retaining wall, six bricked up: one of only two public shelters dug into the hill.
sights.when: Visible from the street, no entry.

sights.name: Parco Leopardi shelter entrances
sights.blurb: Four walled-up shelter mouths marked 'P.A.A.' (Protezione Anti Aerea).

sights.name: Porta Nuova deportation plaque
sights.blurb: 'Partirono da questa stazione i deportati politici per i campi di sterminio nazisti…'
sights.q: Stazione Porta Nuova, Via Sacchi, Torino

sights.name: Pietre d'inciampo, Via Po 25
sights.blurb: Stones for Michele Valabrega and Maria Irene Roscetti, deported on Primo Levi's convoy. Turin has 130: also Piazza Castello 161 (the Colombo family), Corso San Maurizio 8, Via San Domenico 0–1.

sights.name: Cascina Marchesa: Grandi Motori plaques
sights.blurb: Two relocated factory plaques; one marks where five worker-partisans fell under German tank fire on 27 April 1945.

sights.name: Museo Diffuso: rescued factory plaques
sights.blurb: Courtyard plaques taken from Fiat Ferriere and Grandi Motori ('…from which the first spark of the revolt…, 18–28 April 1945').
sights.q: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza, Corso Valdocco 4, Torino

sights.name: Superga: the Grande Torino crash wall
sights.blurb: The basilica's rear retaining wall, still marked by the 4 May 1949 impact that killed the Grande Torino team, with the marble plaque of victims.
sights.q: Lapide Grande Torino, Basilica di Superga, Torino

sights.name: Hotel Roma: Pavese's room 346
sights.blurb: The working hotel where Cesare Pavese was found dead in room 346 on 27 August 1950.
sights.q: Hotel Roma e Rocca Cavour, Piazza Carlo Felice 60, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Cavour plaque
sights.blurb: 1861 marble: Cavour was born in this house on 10 August 1810 and died here on 6 June 1861.

sights.name: Cinema Statuto memorial
sights.blurb: A garden bed and plaque for the 64 who died behind chained exits in the fire of 13 February 1983, which led to Italy's cinema fire law.

sights.name: Arsenale: Paolo Sacchi plaque
sights.blurb: 1886 bronze for the sergeant who kept 40,000 kg of powder from exploding on 26 April 1852, when the magazine blast damaged every house in Borgo Dora.
sights.when: Always visible (now Sermig's Arsenale della Pace).
sights.q: Arsenale della Pace, Piazza Borgo Dora 61, Torino

sights.name: Rousseau's abjuration, Spirito Santo
sights.blurb: Where the 16-year-old Rousseau was registered at the Catecumeni hospice in April 1728 and abjured Calvinism. He later served as a footman in Palazzo Solaro (now MAO, Via San Domenico 11).
sights.q: Chiesa dello Spirito Santo, Via Porta Palatina 9, Torino

sights.name: Guglia Beccaria (geodetic baseline)
sights.blurb: The 1808 obelisk on the end-stone of Beccaria's 1760 baseline for measuring a degree of meridian. Its twin stands 11.8 km west at Rivoli. The black-magic stories are myth.

sights.name: Rivoli twin obelisk
sights.blurb: The western end of Beccaria's baseline, inaugurated 8 October 1808, with a 1934 plaque in the pavement by the newsstand at the start of Via Fratelli Piol.

sights.name: Sobrero nitroglycerine plaque
sights.blurb: 'In the old chemical laboratory of this building Ascanio Sobrero… first realised the synthesis of nitroglycerine' (1846–47). His monument is in the Valentino.

sights.name: Ex-Ospizio di Carità: 1896 Lumière show
sights.blurb: Where Calcina showed about twenty Lumière shorts on 7 November 1896, often called Italy's first public screening (Rome disputes it).

sights.name: Old university, Via Po 17
sights.blurb: The 1714–20 university courtyard where Beccaria taught physics; the 1904 fire here burned the National Library's manuscripts and launched library chemistry.

sights.name: Palazzo Madama observatory tower
sights.blurb: The west tower held the city observatory 1822–1912 until electric lights ruined the sky; the dome went in 1920.
sights.when: Nothing left; look up at the tower.

sights.name: Ambrosio film studios
sights.blurb: Fenoglio's 1911–13 office block and glass-roofed stage of Italy's biggest silent-film studio, now Teatro Espace.

sights.name: Itala Film site
sights.blurb: Pastrone's studio behind Cabiria (1914), built 1906–15. Whether anything survives is unconfirmed.

sights.name: Cinema Nuovo Romano
sights.blurb: A working cinema in the 1870s Galleria Subalpina, with a Lumière room in the basement from 1905.

sights.name: Fiat's first plant, Corso Dante
sights.blurb: The 1899–1900 Fiat buildings, centre of the September 1920 factory occupations, bombed in 1942, now lofts.

sights.name: Palazzo Bricherasio
sights.blurb: Where Fiat's founding deed was signed in July 1899. No Fiat plaque outside (only one for the poet Berchet).

sights.name: Carpano vermouth plaque
sights.blurb: 'Nel 1786 in questa casa creò il suo Vermouth…' The shop is documented; inventing vermouth is tradition.
sights.q: Piazza Castello at Via Viotti, Torino

sights.name: Juventus founding bench
sights.blurb: A bench repainted black-and-white in July 2025 with a plaque, opposite where the club was founded in 1897; the original is in the J Museum.
sights.q: Corso Re Umberto at Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, Torino

sights.name: Bar Norman (Torino FC founded)
sights.blurb: Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine of the then Birreria Voigt on 3 December 1906; plaque and founders' photo inside.
sights.q: Bar Norman, Via Pietro Micca 22, Torino

sights.name: Michelin chimney, Parco Dora
sights.blurb: The stamping-shop chimney, all that is left of Michelin's first Italian plant (1906).

sights.name: Lagrange birthplace
sights.blurb: A faded plaque: Lagrange was born here on 25 January 1736. He later chaired the metric-system commission.

sights.name: Anatomy, Lombroso and Fruit museums
sights.blurb: Three 19th-century museums in one building: Rolando's anatomy rooms, Lombroso's criminal anthropology (discredited science, which is why it matters) and Garnier Valletti's artificial fruits.
sights.q: Museo Lombroso, Via Pietro Giuria 15, Torino

sights.name: Regia Farmacia Masino (1667)
sights.blurb: A pharmacy trading since 1667, with 18th-century fittings, jars and a bronze mortar of 1718.
sights.q: Farmacia Masino, Via Maria Vittoria 3, Torino

sights.name: Farmacia Anglesio
sights.blurb: In the same family since 1682: big historic sign and original fittings. The Farmacia della Consolata (Via delle Orfane 25) is nearby.

sights.name: L'Ordine Nuovo plaque
sights.blurb: 1949 plaque where Gramsci's L'Ordine Nuovo was written; later Einaudi's first offices.

sights.name: Teatro Nuovo: the march of the 40,000
sights.blurb: On 14 October 1980 a Fiat supervisors' meeting here overflowed into the silent march that ended the 35-day strike.
sights.q: Teatro Nuovo, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 17, Torino

sights.name: Ex Capamianto asbestos factory
sights.blurb: 1911–1952 asbestos-factory buildings, 'of documentary interest' in the 1984 census.
sights.q: Corso Peschiera at Via Sant'Antonino, Torino

sights.name: Galileo Ferraris IEEE Milestone
sights.blurb: IEEE plaque for the rotating field and early induction motors (1885–88), dedicated 2021.
sights.when: Energy Center entrance hall; may have moved to the Politecnico (Sala Emma Strada).
sights.q: Energy Center, Via Paolo Borsellino 38, Torino

sights.name: Lavazza's first shop
sights.blurb: Luigi Lavazza's 1895 grocery where he began blending coffee, now a café with company photos.
sights.q: San Tommaso 10, Via San Tommaso 10, Torino

sights.name: Lancia's first workshop
sights.blurb: Founded 27 November 1906 at the corner of Via Ormea and Via Donizetti; the doors reportedly had to be widened to get the first car out.
sights.q: Via Ormea at Via Donizetti, Torino

sights.name: Aeritalia airfield: first airmail
sights.blurb: On 22 May 1917 De Bernardi flew the world's first airmail from the Pomilio field here to Rome. Still Aero Club Torino's field.

sights.name: University Botanic Garden
sights.blurb: The 1729 royal garden by the Valentino castle, with old Ginkgo, cedar and yew.
sights.when: Sat 14:30–19, Sun 10–19 late Mar–mid Nov, €5; closed for winter from ~17 Nov.

sights.name: Regional Natural Sciences Museum
sights.blurb: In the former San Giovanni hospital; closed after a 2013 explosion, partly reopened January 2024.
sights.when: Partly open; more works approved Oct 2026.
sights.q: Museo Regionale di Scienze Naturali, Via Giolitti 36, Torino

sights.name: Primo Levi's house
sights.blurb: Primo Levi's birth and death house; his surname still on the doorbell.

sights.name: SOMS Edmondo De Amicis
sights.blurb: A still-active workers' mutual-aid society club, with banners and members' photos on the walls.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Piazza Villari
sights.blurb: A Liberty-era cast-stone urinal stamped 'U. Renzi', one of the two oldest of about 29 survivors, repainted in pastels as street art.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Piazza Sassari
sights.blurb: The other Liberty-style Renzi kiosk on little columns.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Corso Regina Margherita
sights.blurb: A classic 1930s curved 'Modello 900' kiosk by the Giardini Reali.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio
sights.blurb: Modello 900 kiosk on the side road before the Teatro Nuovo.

sights.name: Vanchiglia public baths (1901)
sights.blurb: A modest Liberty bathhouse by Dolza that still works as public baths, run by volunteers.
sights.q: Bagni pubblici, Corso Regina Margherita 33, Torino

sights.name: Ex-bagni, Via Morgari (San Salvario)
sights.blurb: Dolza's Liberty bathhouse with curving wings and a cornice of alternating frogs and shells, now the Casa del Quartiere café.
sights.q: Casa del Quartiere di San Salvario, Via Morgari 14, Torino

sights.name: Ex-bagni of San Donato (1900)
sights.blurb: The district's first shower baths and wash-house with zoomorphic decoration, now a library.

sights.name: Via Agliè public baths (1956)
sights.blurb: A working 1956 bathhouse in Barriera di Milano that replaced baths in a demolished toll house.

sights.name: Via Cherasco public baths
sights.blurb: An early-20th-century bathhouse whose eight showers still run.

sights.name: 1912 toll house, Piazza Rebaudengo
sights.blurb: The yellow 1912 customs office of the northern gate, in its original form, with a flying-ship mural. The big 'barrier' squares exist because the gates stood there.

sights.name: Toll house, Piazza Stampalia
sights.blurb: 1912 toll quarters of the Barriera di Lanzo, now a district meeting centre.

sights.name: Toll house, Piazza Bengasi
sights.blurb: The 1912 customs house on the Moncalieri border, nearly lost to Metro 1 and restored in original colours in 2023.

sights.name: Ice-houses in the Mercato Centrale
sights.blurb: Two 19th-century underground ice chambers found in 2002, left open to view in a sunken plaza of Fuksas's market hall: domes, drainage floors, roof hatches.
sights.when: Free in building hours; layout changes, check.
sights.q: Mercato Centrale, Piazza della Repubblica 25, Torino

sights.name: Po flood column
sights.blurb: The column by the Borgo Medievale recording the great floods: highest October 1839 at 6.20 m; 2000 and 2016 within 30–50 cm.

sights.name: Museo dei Lavandai, Bertolla
sights.blurb: Turin's laundry village (1872–1960s): washing tools, the kneeling 'scagn', photos.
sights.q: Museo dei Lavandai, Strada Comunale di Bertolla 113, Torino

sights.name: Sassi–Superga rack tramway
sights.blurb: The 1884 line (rack since 1935) climbing 3.1 km at up to 21% in 1934 cars; Sassi station keeps a small history room.
sights.when: Hourly 10–18 from Sassi in season, no service Wed; winter suspensions. Check gtt.to.it.

sights.name: Ponte Mosca
sights.blurb: A single flat stone arch over the Dora, 45 m span and only 5.5 m rise (1823–30), 'a unicum' of early 19th-century stone bridges.
sights.when: Best from the Lungo Dora path.
sights.q: Ponte Mosca, Corso Giulio Cesare, Torino

sights.name: Old Torino–Ceres terminus
sights.blurb: The 1869 terminus of the Lanzo Valleys railway, disused since 1986.

sights.name: Duomo meridian line
sights.blurb: A noon line on the cathedral's side wall marking the zodiac, with a star-shaped gnomon: an ordinary sundial, not an anti-Church code.
sights.when: Go near solar noon (about 12:20, 13:20 in summer time).
sights.q: Duomo di Torino, Piazza San Giovanni, Torino

sights.name: Fountain of seven torèt
sights.blurb: Seven of Turin's 800 green bull-head fountains in a semicircle. The 'lovers' pair faces off at Via Stampatori 4.

sights.name: Brass bull of Piazza San Carlo
sights.blurb: The rearing bull set in the arcade pavement; spin on its testicles for luck.

sights.name: 'Columbus's finger'
sights.blurb: Students rub Columbus's finger for luck; the bronze is actually Somà's 1923 memorial to Latin-American Italian WWI volunteers.

sights.name: Frejus tunnel monument
sights.blurb: A pyramid of real rocks from the 1871 tunnel dig with Titans and a winged Genius of Science (1879). The 'Lucifer' is a legend.
sights.q: Monumento al Traforo del Frejus, Piazza Statuto, Torino

sights.name: Portone del Diavolo
sights.blurb: A 1675 Parisian door with a gilded devil-head knocker. Same corner: the 'Horns of Pan' mask; more masks at Via Alfieri 15.
sights.when: Always visible; the ghosts are legend.
sights.q: Palazzo Trucchi di Levaldigi, Via XX Settembre 40, Torino

sights.name: Torre Littoria
sights.blurb: Turin's first 'grattanuvole' (1933–34, 87 m), meant as the Fascist HQ: 'il dito del Duce'. Its own plaque gives the wrong dates.

sights.name: T'oro: bull bursting from a wall
sights.blurb: Richi Ferrero's half bull with golden horns smashing out of brick.

sights.name: Upside-down David
sights.blurb: Salvatori's red David head upside down in Palazzo Villa's courtyard passage.
sights.q: Palazzo Villa, Piazza San Carlo, Torino

sights.name: Lampioni innamorati bench
sights.blurb: An iron bench where two street lamps sit, one leaning on the other (Marasciuolo, 2002).
sights.q: Giardino Roccioso, Parco del Valentino, Torino

sights.name: Submarine 'Andrea Provana'
sights.blurb: The central section of a 1915–18 submarine, placed in the Valentino in 1933.
sights.q: Sommergibile Provana, Viale Marinai d'Italia, Torino

sights.name: Palace of the bats
sights.blurb: Two big stone bats under the third-floor balconies (1876).

sights.name: Smallest piazzetta
sights.blurb: About 17 × 13 m with its own sign and number; Cavour's funeral was held in its church.
sights.q: Piazzetta Beata Vergine degli Angeli, Torino

sights.name: Via Ercole Ricotti: shortest street
sights.blurb: About 23–30 m long with two house numbers on two mirror buildings. The narrowest, vicolo Santa Maria, is 2.85 m.

sights.name: Lost Torre Civica
sights.blurb: The civic tower stood here 1379–1801, with a gilded bull on the spire and the first public clock (1387); demolished to straighten Via Garibaldi.
sights.q: Via Garibaldi at Via San Francesco d'Assisi, Torino

offmap.name: Cesana Pariol bobsleigh/luge track
offmap.blurb: A long zig-zag "serpentone" of concrete and sheet metal down a larch slope, with refrigeration plant and stands. It is the nearest thing in Italy to Sarajevo's Trebević track.
offmap.when: €9M has been allocated for (partial) demolition and "rinaturalizzazione".
offmap.q: Pista di bob Cesana Pariol, Cesana Torinese

offmap.name: Pragelato Olympic ski jumps
offmap.blurb: Five jumps (HS106 and HS140 Olympic hills), a judges' tower and an abandoned hotel at the foot. The jumps' green plastic summer matting is disintegrating, and one 2025 visitor called it an ecological "time bomb".
offmap.when: The area below the jumps is being converted for biathlon and roller-skiing (≈€5M, Universiade works, permanent facility targeted for winter 2026–27). The jumps themselves are being kept, not demolished ("troppo caro smontarli").

offmap.name: Ivrea
offmap.blurb: Talponia is a semicircular, half-buried "horizontal skyscraper" about 300 m long, with 82 duplex and simplex cells facing a hillside under a grass roof. Beyond it, the Via Jervis axis: Figini & Pollini's ICO works and social services, Gino Valle's offices, the open-air MaAM, and the all-concrete Sacro Cuore church (Favini structures).
offmap.when: Talponia is lived in, so walk past respectfully. UNESCO Visitor Centre, Via Jervis 11: free, Tue–Sun 10–18 until 15 Nov 2026; weekend tours at 10:00 and 15:00. ICO and the social-services building inside only on guided tours.

offmap.name: Mollino's Lago Nero sled station
offmap.blurb: Mollino's 1946–47 sled-lift station at 2,286 m above Sauze d'Oulx, restored 1999–2005, now a ski-season refuge.
offmap.when: On foot from Pian della Rocca via Sportinia in summer, by lifts in winter. Check the season (0122 858009).
offmap.q: Chalet Mollino, Lago Nero, Sauze d'Oulx

offmap.name: Forte di Fenestrelle
offmap.blurb: A fortress chain climbing the mountainside in Val Chisone, billed as Europe's longest fortification.
offmap.when: Guided only, booking by phone; routes 1, 3 or 7 h ('Passeggiata Reale' €20). Winter hours vary.

offmap.name: Forte di Exilles
offmap.blurb: The 1830 fortress of Val di Susa with galleries and underground passages.
offmap.when: Season 20 Jun–27 Sep; special opening 31 Oct 2026. Exterior visible from the SS24.

offmap.name: Orco dams: Ceresole and Serrù
offmap.blurb: Ceresole's 1931 concrete gravity dam (52 m, 302 m crest) in Gran Paradiso park, with the Serrù and Agnel dams above 2,000 m on the Nivolet road, and the Rosone power station below.
offmap.when: Ceresole visible year-round; the high road closes in winter (summer 2027 target).

offmap.name: Mont-Cenis: dam and Vallo Alpino forts
offmap.blurb: France's largest rockfill dam (1.4 km, 120 m) and the 1933–42 Italian strongpoints of the Vallo Alpino around the pass: caves, firing posts, steel cupolas.
offmap.when: Summer only; forts entered entirely at your own risk (torch, stay on paths). French territory since 1947.

offmap.name: Valle Stura Vallo Alpino and Vinadio
offmap.blurb: Opera 5 'San Membotto' with the only mortar block on the western Alps, and the Forte di Vinadio's 'Caverna Comando'.
offmap.when: Trail-side works; Vinadio by guided route. A long day trip into Cuneo province.

offmap.name: Fabbrica della Ruota, Pray
offmap.blurb: An 1878 wool mill with its water-power transmission, machinery and 2 km of archives, on the Biella 'Strada della Lana'.
offmap.when: Summer Sundays 14:30–18:30 to end Oct, €5; after October by appointment (351 3902199).
offmap.q: Fabbrica della Ruota, Regione Vallefredda 1, Pray

p: A square hall the size of a city block, roofed by sixteen freestanding concrete "mushroom" columns, each crowned with a steel umbrella. The glass and metal walls between them are rusting and broken, so from Corso Unità d'Italia you can see straight into the forest of columns. It is the southern gateway to the city, and its biggest ruin.

Pier Luigi Nervi won the 1959 competition and built it with his son Antonio, Gino Covre on the steel, and Gio Ponti, for Italia '61, the centenary of Italian unification. It opened with Ponti's exhibition "Man at Work", and a monorail ran from here to the Palazzo delle Mostre. Later it held a university faculty until 2008, then the odd disco and event, then nothing. It is listed by the heritage authority.

Its future keeps stalling. CDP Immobiliare has owned it since 2020 and finished safety works in early 2025. A shopping-centre plan was dropped, and a rumoured Qatari cultural investment of about €500M was described as stuck by April 2026: the mayor blamed the war in Iran for scaring off investors, while the urbanism assessor said he knew of no concrete talks. An October 2026 op-ed claims it will not be restored at all. Expect it to still be a ruin when you visit.
It is fenced and structurally damaged, so don't go in. The best views are from Corso Unità d'Italia and Via Ventimiglia. The monorail stumps and the Italia '61 fountain are a short walk away.

Nervi's great ferrocement vault of 1948–50, once called a "modern cathedral", built from prefabricated pieces like a giant ribbed shell. Under it lies Morandi's 1959 underground hall. Rafael Moneo has restored the whole complex as Turin's new central library, putting most of the new rooms below ground so the vault stays one open space.

Ettore Sottsass Sr. built the first exhibition complex here in 1938. It was bombed, and Nervi rebuilt it as an exhibition hall; early editions of the Turin Book Fair were held under the vault. The restoration is a roughly €166M project funded by the EU recovery plan. The city gives 20,000 m² of floor space, which would make it one of the largest public libraries in Italy; the culture assessor quoted 24,000 m², 1,000 study seats and 150,000 books on open shelves.

The opening kept slipping, from June 2026 to "autumn". The mayor has now announced 11 December 2026 as the public opening, with events starting in November. It was still closed on 20 October 2026. As a public library it should be free. Before December you can only see the outside, from Corso Massimo d'Azeglio and the Valentino park.
esposizioni.s: Comune di Torino (Jul 2026); Quotidiano Piemontese (Jan 2026); Exibart

p: A long zig-zag of concrete and sheet metal snaking down a larch slope, with its refrigeration plant and empty stands. This is the Torino 2006 bobsleigh and luge track, and it is the closest thing in Italy to Sarajevo's abandoned Trebević track.

It cost €110M and seated 7,130 people. Armin Zöggeler never lost on it and won one of Italy's five home golds here. Afterwards it lost €1.3–1.5M a year to run and closed around 2011–12. In 2023 Italy proposed reviving it for the Milano-Cortina 2026 games, and the IOC refused, pointing out it had already been abandoned once.

Its days are numbered. €9M has been set aside for partial demolition and returning the slope to nature, and the government commissioner said in 2025 that works would start in summer 2026. It was still standing in July 2026, and I found no report that work has begun. Expect fencing, and check local news (Luna Nuova, ValsusaOggi) before the trip in case it is a building site.
Pair it with the Pragelato ski jumps in the next valley; those are being kept.
cesana.s: Eco del Chisone (Apr 2025); Luna Nuova; ValsusaOggi

p: Five Olympic ski jumps standing in a row above Val Chisone, with a judges' tower and an abandoned hotel at the foot. In summer you see the green plastic matting on the landing slopes falling apart; one visitor in 2025 called it an ecological time bomb.
The jumps cost about €34M for Torino 2006. Tubing and summer jumping were tried afterwards and failed, and the Olympic hills don't even belong to the town.

Unlike Cesana, they are not coming down: it is too expensive to dismantle them. The area below is being rebuilt for biathlon and roller-skiing (about €5M, aimed at winter 2026–27), so expect building sites under the jumps.
pragelato.s: Report on Turin's Olympic sites, Oct 2026 (local press)

p: Olivetti's company town, a UNESCO site since 2018. The star is Talponia, a half-buried "horizontal skyscraper": a 300 m crescent of 82 flats cut into a hillside under a grass roof, so from above you see only a lawn. In the centre, Hotel La Serra by Cappai and Mainardis is a sculptural concrete block of the late 1960s.

Olivetti commissioned Talponia from Gabetti and Isola in 1968 to house visiting staff, and it was finished in late 1970. La Serra's excavation turned up Roman remains. Along Via Jervis you can follow the whole Olivetti story: Figini and Pollini's glass-walled ICO works and their social-services building, Gino Valle's 1980s offices, and the open-air MaAM museum with seven stations. Nearby, the Sacro Cuore church is all concrete, its thin walls planted in the ground like blades.

Talponia is lived in, so walk past quietly. One flat is a private Olivetti house-museum; check its terms. The new UNESCO Visitor Centre at Via Jervis 11 opened on 12 September 2026: free, Tue–Sun 10–18 until 15 November, with weekend guided walks at 10:00 and 15:00 (the Welcome Tours take about 2.5 hours). Ivrea is about an hour from Turin by train, and it is the best single concrete day trip.
ivrea.s: UNESCO / Ivrea Visitor Centre; idealista/news (Sep 2026); MiC Censimento

p: A banked car test track on the roof of a factory, 28 m above the street. Fiat built cars floor by floor going up through the Lingotto and drove them out on top. Today the track is a planted garden of about 40,000 plants, with Renzo Piano's glass "Bubble" and the Pinacoteca's "treasure chest" perched on the roof.

The 1920s building is a key monument of Italian concrete industrial architecture, and the rooftop track is one of the most famous images of modern Italy. It is a tourist icon, so lower priority, but it is still pure odd infrastructure.

Go up through the Pinacoteca Agnelli, open Tue–Sun 10–19 (schedule valid to 28 October 2026; check after). Track only costs €4 (€2 reduced); with the gallery €12 (€8). It sometimes closes early for private events.

Mario Botta's seven-towered brick church, built in 2004–06 on the site of Fiat's steelworks. The old 60 m steelworks chimney was kept as the bell tower, wrapped in a steel spiral with a cross on top. Next door, Parco Dora keeps the steel skeletons of the factory sheds and the old cooling tanks as a park.

It was the first church built in Turin this century and is now the city's co-cathedral. The chimney was kept on purpose, as a memory of the workers of this "city of labour". Oddly, the bells actually hang at its base.
The church is an active parish, free, open around services. The park is public and always open. The Michelin chimney, the last trace of another factory, is also in Parco Dora.
santovolto.s: Report on Turin's concrete sites, Oct 2026

p: A cemetery that looks like a landscape: about 69 hectares of rolling lawns with the Alps behind. The concrete burial blocks are hidden under artificial hills, and the graves are simple slabs flush with the grass. It also has Islamic, Evangelical and Romanian Orthodox sections, with an Orthodox chapel.

It was built in 1969–72, when the Monumentale had filled up during the boom of migration to the Fiat factories. Its designers deliberately copied the Nordic "park cemetery", in what has been called egalitarian modernism. A memorial to the Cinema Statuto fire victims is here too.
Municipal and free; check the opening hours on the city website.

Three parallel concrete galleries, each about 40 m long, 12 m under Piazza Risorgimento, with walls 80 cm thick. The wartime rules of conduct are still painted on the walls. Up in the square, the entrance turrets now carry murals by the artist XEL.
It was one of about 45 public shelters built in 1942–44. Turin was bombed from 12 June 1940 to 5 April 1945, and 2,069 people died.

It opens only on special days: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza tours, FAI days and Monumenti Aperti. Book through the Museo Diffuso (011 01120780). If you miss it, the shelter under Le Nuove prison runs regular guided tours, and the one under the town hall also opens for visits.
rifugio.s: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza; Monumenti Aperti

p: Sixteen identical eight-storey slabs, 652 flats in heavy prefab, lined up in rows to catch the sun. Designed by Nello Renacco in the late 1960s, this is Turin's nearest thing to a Falowiec or an Aillaud estate: not in scale, but in spirit.

It was built for the southern migrants who came to work at Fiat. Its tenants' committee is one of the oldest in the city and celebrated 50 years in 2017. The 2020 book *Abitare i margini* tells its story of 1970s housing struggles.
Lived-in social housing: look from the street.
taranto.s: Abitare i margini (2020). Map pin approximate

p: A single nave of bare brick under a folded, faceted roof of exposed concrete. Built in 1955–57 by Nicola and Leonardo Mosso in Mirafiori Nord, it is considered Nicola Mosso's key church and became the model for others: the churches at Moriondo and Nichelino copy its roof.
Leonardo Mosso later became a well-known collaborator of Alvar Aalto. The roof was restored in 2002. It is an active parish, so go around Mass times to see inside.

A brick-clad tower on Piazza Statuto with jutting bay windows and arcades at its foot, by the Milan firm BBPR for the insurer Reale Mutua. It is Turin's cousin of their Torre Velasca in Milan: modern, but deliberately heavy and historical-looking.
The dates are disputed: 1955–59 in one source, 1959–61 in another. It is offices, so outside only. The Guglia Beccaria and the Frejus monument are in the same square.

A marble plaque at Via Carlo Alberto 6 marks where Nietzsche spent his last lucid months. His room was the fifth window from the corner on the fourth floor, above the Galleria Subalpina entrance. He loved Turin, and here he wrote *Ecce Homo* and finished *Twilight of the Idols*.

He stayed from 21 September 1888 to 9 January 1889, paying 30 lire a month to the newsagent Davide Fino. On 3 January 1889 he collapsed in the street. The famous story that he threw his arms around a beaten horse is disputed: most sources put it in Piazza Carlo Alberto, just outside, one puts it in Piazza San Carlo, and several call it more legend than fact. It inspired Béla Tarr's film *The Turin Horse*.
The flat is private; the plaque is always visible. Palazzo Campana is a few doors down, and Del Cambio and Palazzo Carignano are round the corner.
nietzsche.s: Report on Turin's thinkers' sites, Oct 2026

p: A grand palazzo a few doors from Nietzsche's plaque, now a university building. It is, according to the Resistance institute Istoreto, the only public building in Turin that still carries the name of a partisan.

Under Fascism it was the party's headquarters, the Casa del Littorio. The Black Brigades held arrested partisans here, and their graffiti stayed on the walls for years. After 1945 it went to the university and was named after the fallen partisan Campana. It is said to have been the centre of the 1967–68 student occupation, though I didn't verify that.
The courtyard is usually open in term time.

Black iron cannonballs set into the plaster of Turin's façades, left there on purpose as memorials of the city's sieges. The easiest to find are the two on the north façade of the courtyard of Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana (Via della Consolata 1 bis), and several around Piazza San Carlo.
Most are French shot from the great siege of 1706. Others are from 1799, when the French garrison holding the Cittadella fired on the city, then taken by Suvorov's Austro-Russian army.

A 2025 local guide lists about ten spots: in Piazza San Carlo, on Palazzo Solaro del Borgo, two on the east side near Via Giolitti, and one in the arcade above the Mokika café; inside the MAO; on the façade of the Oratorio di San Filippo Neri in Via Maria Vittoria; on the building north of Via Palazzo di Città in Piazza Palazzo di Città; on the west wall of the Aula di Sant'Andrea at the Consolata; and three at Santa Maria del Monte (Cappuccini), inside above the San Fedele niche, on the convent façade by the Massaia plaque, and on the church front.
It becomes a treasure hunt. The Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana courtyard is reachable in business hours.
cannonballs.s: GuidaTorino (2025); Piemonte Italia. Map pin approximate

p: A tall, thin, wedge-shaped house whose narrow end is only 54 cm wide. Turin calls it the "slice of polenta". It was built by Alessandro Antonelli, the architect of the Mole, who seems to have enjoyed pushing a building as far as it would go.
It is a private building, so view it from the street, at the corner of Corso San Maurizio and Via Giulia di Barolo.
fetta.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026

p: A tiny Liberty-style café of 31 m² on Piazza Castello, all wood, mirrors and marble. Inside, a plaque says that in 1926 Signora Angela Demichelis Nebiolo invented the tramezzino here, the white-bread triangle sandwich now found all over Italy.

The name tramezzino is credited to Gabriele D'Annunzio, and sources give 1925 or 1926. The café has been a listed historic shop since 1985. It opens roughly 09:30–20:00 (19:30 on Tue and Wed). Have a tramezzino at the counter: that is the point.
Guarini's baroque palace with its rippling brick façade. Behind it is the hall where Italy's first parliament proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. It now houses the Museo del Risorgimento.

It is a famous sight, so lower priority, but it is the anchor of a tight cluster: Del Cambio is opposite, and Nietzsche's plaque and Palazzo Campana are a minute away. Check the museum's current hours and prices before going.

A small plaque in Piazza San Carlo for the victims of the night of 3 June 2017. Thousands were watching the Juventus Champions League final on a big screen when a robbery gang sprayed pepper spray, and the crowd panicked and stampeded.
Three people eventually died and hundreds were hurt. Four people were convicted of manslaughter. The plaque was placed in 2019.
sancarlo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: Look up at the fourth-floor corner of Piazzetta Corpus Domini 19: an oversized metal ring pierces the corner of an 18th-century building, like an earring. It was a temporary art installation, *Baci Urbani* ("urban kisses"), that was simply never taken down. A small joke on an old building.
baci.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026

p: A restaurant open since 1757, facing Palazzo Carignano. In the main room, the table where Count Cavour used to sit is still kept and marked with a small plaque. From it he could watch the parliament across the square, ready to run over if he was needed.

This is one of the best documented "sit where he sat" places in Turin; both the regional tourism site and Rolling Stone Italia confirm the table. The longer lists of famous guests (Casanova, Puccini, Balzac, Nietzsche, Verdi) are promotional and unverified.
It has a Michelin star and is expensive. Dinner runs roughly 19:30–23:30, with Sunday lunch, and there is a cheaper bistro at lunch. You can ask for Cavour's table when you book (delcambio.it).

A café on the corner of Piazza Vittorio Veneto with its original red breccia-marble tables. Cesare Pavese spent his time writing here, and the city itself says you can have breakfast where he wrote. It is the best documented of the "Pavese" cafés.
Giuseppe Carpano is said to have perfected his vermouth here around 1889–1902, so a vermouth is the fitting order. A blog claims Nietzsche "certainly" came here; there is no evidence for it.
Open Mon–Fri 08–00 (closed Wednesday), Sat 09–01, Sun 09–00.

The café of the Risorgimento establishment, open since 1780 on Via Po. Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo, Santorre di Santarosa and Cavour came here, and Cavour is said to have founded his Whist Club in its rooms. It was the conservative café, while San Carlo was the patriots'.

King Carlo Alberto supposedly asked his ministers "What are they saying at Fiorio?", to take the pulse of the court. Nietzsche is linked to it through its ice cream; plausible, but only popular sources say so.
It's at Via Po 8; one guide gives a wrong address on Piazza Castello. Check hours.

A tiny café of 1763 facing the Consolata sanctuary, where the bicerin was born: coffee, chocolate and cream layered in a small glass. By long tradition Cavour drank here while waiting for the royal family to leave Mass at the Consolata.

The famous names on the walls (Dumas, Puccini, Nietzsche, Gozzano, Calvino) are tradition, and even the Cavour story is usually told as "legend has it". The firmest literary link is fictional: Umberto Eco set a scene of *The Prague Cemetery* here.
Closed Wednesdays; roughly 08:30–19:30. It's tiny, so expect a queue. The Consolata has cannonballs in one wall, and the Farmacia della Consolata is nearby.
A grand café of 1822 on Piazza San Carlo, the meeting place of Risorgimento patriots: D'Azeglio, Cavour, Rattazzi, Giolitti, Crispi. The police closed it several times on suspicion of subversion.

A literary circle met here in the 1920s. In 1899 the Duke of the Abruzzi is said to have planned his polar expedition here (sources say "Antarctic", but the voyage went to the Arctic). The line that Gramsci conceived *L'Ordine Nuovo* here is a stock marketing phrase with no scholarly source.
Open roughly 08:00–00:00. It was closed for restoration in 1953–63, and the management has changed several times.
An 1870s café on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II with a gilded interior. Popular sources list Luigi Einaudi, Cesare Pavese, Natalia Ginzburg and the founders of Fiat and Lavazza among its regulars.

It has a bumpy history: it went bankrupt and closed in 2015 before reopening, and changed owners again in September 2026. The new owners closed it for restyling and, according to ANSA and the café's own site, reopened it to the public on 23 October 2026. Worth a look to see how they treated the old rooms.
The Royal Library under the Musei Reali: Pelagio Palagi's long vaulted hall, founded by Carlo Alberto in 1831–37. It holds Leonardo's drawings, including his famous red-chalk self-portrait.

I found no sourced list of famous readers, so this is a "sit in a great reading room" stop rather than a "sat where X sat" one. Until 6 January 2027 the hall also hosts an exhibition on Queen Margherita.

Tourists see the hall with a Musei Reali ticket: Mon and Fri 9:00–13:30; Tue, Thu and Sat 13:30–18:30. The reading room is for adult researchers only, booked by email at least 24 hours ahead (Mon and Fri 13:30–18:30; Tue, Thu and Sat 8:30–13:30; closed Wednesday).

The library of Turin's Academy of Sciences, founded in 1783 with Lagrange among its founders. Its early members included Monge, Laplace, d'Alembert and Euler. It also keeps a pair of Coronelli globes.
Turin's first proper observatory was built on this roof in 1790; nothing of it survives.
Visits are by appointment only (Mon–Thu 9–13 and 15–17, Fri 9–13, through a form). Casual visitors usually get in only during events and talks.

From Piazza Castello you see only Juvarra's old baroque front. Behind it Carlo Mollino built an entirely new theatre in brick and concrete: curving foyers, an oval hall, and below ground the tailoring workshop, ballet room and the small Piccolo Regio. It is Mollino's largest building.
The 1740 theatre burned in February 1936, leaving only the façade. Mollino's replacement took until 1973 to open.

The backstage tours ("Il Regio dietro le quinte") last an hour: Sat 15:00 and 16:30, Sun 11:00, except holidays and show days. €10 (€5 under 18), Italian only, max 25 people. Tickets go on sale online from the Monday before each month's first tour, so book early.
With the Palazzo degli Affari and the Lago Nero sled station, it makes a Mollino thread across the map.

The Chamber of Commerce by Carlo Mollino and partners, 1964–73: a block raised on a single central core, a four-storey "blade" linked to it by a walkway in the air, and inside, Mollino's helical staircase.

They won a 1964 competition against 29 teams, on the site of a palace destroyed by bombs. During building the central pylon and the gap above the base were made smaller, which hides some of the original daring.
It's working public offices, so you can usually step in during opening hours. The architecture foundation has run occasional paid tours (€6). The Ex Borsa is next door.
affari.s: Camera di commercio Torino; TorinoToday; MiC Censimento

p: The old stock exchange: a trading hall under a distinctive vaulted concrete roof, facing Piazzale Valdo Fusi. Gabetti, Isola and Raineri won the 1953 competition and built it in 1952–56; it is an early key work of their generation.
Trading ended in 1992 and it has been shut ever since. A €14.6M conversion is planned, but works may not start until 2028, with completion around 2030. For now, outside only.
borsa.s: MuseoTorino; Torino Oggi (Sep 2026). Map pin approximate

p: The university's humanities building of the 1960s: a hulking slab on an exposed steel frame, one of the first of its kind in Turin. Steel, not concrete, but brutal in mass, and the campus monolith of the 1968 generation.
Felice Bardelli, one of its designers, also built the Gesù Operaio church. It's open in university hours, but expect closures during protests: it was occupied and shut for a week in early 2026.
A block of flats that seems to ripple: undulating façades banded in cast "litocemento", and an entrance shaped like an oyster shell with concave steps. Inside, no two floor plans are the same.
Sergio Jaretti and Elio Luzi built it in 1954–59 as a provocation, with nods to Gaudí and Wright. It became the icon of Turin's Neoliberty movement. Private flats, so look from Piazza Crimea.
Two ten-storey towers that stand on a forest of pillars and grow heavier as they rise, with deep balconies you could live on. They look as if they were built upside down.
Jaretti and Luzi (1962–68) did it on purpose: they found a loophole in the 1959 zoning rules and moved the floor area upwards, where it was worth more.

Private, outside only; Open House Torino has sometimes opened them. Other Jaretti and Luzi housing to drive past: Corso Orbassano 268, Via Curtatone 3, Via Breglio/Via Bibiana, Piazza Rebaudengo (1966) and Piazza Statuto (1958–59).
pitagora.s: MuseoTorino; MiC Censimento; Open House Italia

p: Turin's first postwar satellite village: three-storey red-brick blocks set out on a hexagonal grid around a civic centre, with a concrete mushroom column at its heart. It was designed by Giovanni Astengo's team in 1951–60.
It was a manifesto of the "organic neighbourhood" ideas that Olivetti promoted. Just north, Falchera Nuova's sixteen 1970s prefab towers show the harsher version that came next.
Public streets. The architecture foundation runs guided walks, meeting at Viale Falchera 80. San Michele Arcangelo is a short walk away.

71 hectares of 1958–68 public housing designed by 45 architects in nine teams, including Gabetti and Isola and Levi Montalcini. Towers, slabs and Scandinavian-style courtyards sit side by side, so it reads like an anthology of 1960s Turin housing.

It was planned for 20,000 people and long carried a bad reputation, but architecturally it is the richest estate in the city. Gabetti and Isola's middle school at Via dei Mughetti 26 breaks the usual school block into pieces.
Public streets. The local history centre gives tours during Open House.
vallette.s: MuseoTorino; Open House Torino; MiC Censimento. Map pin approximate

p: An all-concrete church on a central plan whose complicated roof rests on massive pillars and seems to float above a continuous ribbon of windows. Built in 1967–69 by the engineer Mario Bianco.
It is one of the churches of Turin's post-Council building boom under Cardinal Pellegrino. Bianco also designed San Francesco di Sales. Active parish; go around Mass times.
A post-Council church whose bell tower and roof dominate the local skyline. In 2010 the Turin architects' order called it one of the most mature church designs of the period.
Dates conflict: 1961 or 1970 (probably the full complex). The liturgical area was altered in 2013. Active parish; pin approximate.
santateresa.s: OAT; CEI Chiese italiane. Map pin approximate

p: A 1963–67 church in Barriera di Milano by the engineer Felice Bardelli, co-designer of Palazzo Nuovo. The church census singles out its structural system, and under the church there is a basketball and volleyball gym.
Consecrated by Cardinal Pellegrino in 1967. Exposed concrete is not confirmed, so check it in person before giving it time.
A 1967–71 church by Mario Federico Roggero, built in the middle of the Mirafiori Sud public housing estates. It is also a venue for the MITO music festival.
Exposed concrete unconfirmed; go at Mass times (Sat 18:15, Sun 9:30, 11:00, 18:15) to see inside. Pair it with the Mirafiori factory front.
sanluca.s: MuseoTorino; Diocese of Turin. Map pin approximate

p: A 1967–70 church by Dolci and Tripodi with a pointed, spire-like roof, a short walk from the Falchera estates. The church census flags its structure as notable.
Materials unconfirmed; a pass-by to check in person.
A 1973–78 church in San Paolo by Mario Bianco, the engineer of the all-concrete San Paolo Apostolo, which makes it worth a look.
Materials unverified; pin approximate.
sanfrancescosales.s: Diocese of Turin catalogue. Map pin approximate

p: A modest 1960s church in Parella by Carbonara and Berardo; even the parish's own blessing text called it small. Only worth it if you pass by.
mariagoretti.s: Parish of Santa Maria Goretti. Map pin approximate

p: In the park by the Italia '61 lake, 14 spans of a 1961 monorail still stand on concrete piers shaped like upside-down pyramids, with the shell of the south station. They lead nowhere: of the original 58 spans, the rest are gone.

The Alweg monorail opened on 6 May 1961 for the centenary exhibition and closed in November 1963, after barely two years. Most of the viaduct was taken down in 1994 after concrete started falling. The train itself burned in the depot in 1979.
Some of the dismantled beams still lie in a field beside the ring road at Nichelino, visible only from the motorway, and others were reported at Collegno; neither is confirmed in 2026.
Freely visible in the public park. Expect graffiti, pigeons, crumbling concrete and some rough sleepers. The abandoned 1961 fountain and the Palazzo del Lavoro are nearby.
monorail.s: MuseoTorino; TorinoStoria; Amici di Italia '61. Map pin approximate

p: The illuminated fountain of the 1961 exhibition, near the Palavela. The Italia '61 volunteer group describes it as still there, though left to itself. Don't confuse it with the fountain at the Valentino entrance.
Not re-checked in 2026; it sits next to the monorail stumps.
fontana61.s: Amici di Italia '61. Map pin approximate

p: The monorail's north station still stands, now Casa UGI, a home for families of children with cancer. The monorail train burned in its depot here on 17 December 1979 and was scrapped.
It's in use, so look from outside and be discreet.
A 69 m red steel arch holding up a 400 m footbridge over the railway yards, the most visible legacy of the 2006 Olympics. It links the 1932 market arcades to the coloured prefab athletes' village.
Parts of the old Olympic village (ex-MOI) were occupied from 2013, and some buildings are still empty or fenced. The footbridge is public.
A 5.5 km sunken railway cutting through northern Turin, abandoned, overgrown and full of dumped rubbish. You see it from bridges and street edges, like a hidden valley through the city.

Not for long. Metro Line 2 will run largely along it: the €1bn tender was published in May 2026, and works on the first section are due to start in the first half of 2027. The plan is three stations and a tree-lined boulevard. Residents held a protest sit-in in October 2026.
See it this winter, from public streets only.
The ruins of OSI-Ghia, a 1960 car-body plant abandoned since 2001. It is fenced, and the local press advises avoiding the area. Exterior only, and only if you are passing.
Vast empty steelworks sheds along Corso Regina Margherita. This is where seven workers died in the ThyssenKrupp fire of December 2007, which a local paper calls an open wound for the city.
Fenced, exterior only. Visit with respect.
The surviving sheds of the factory where Superga's canvas sneakers were made, abandoned since 1998.
In July 2026 the city announced a deal to turn it into a culture hub run by Paratissima (€3.5M, about three years of works). Until then, outside only.
superga_f.s: Torino Cronaca; Torino Oggi (Jul 2026). Map pin approximate

p: The Officine Grandi Motori, a 70,000 m² Fiat engine works emptied from 1971. What's left are dramatic shells: the 1911 "Basilica" hall and the "Lingottino", seen from Corso Vigevano and Corso Vercelli around a fenced demolition site.

Demolition started in February 2025 and has been slowed by stability checks. The Basilica will become shops and the Lingottino student housing, with a garden and an Esselunga logistics hub. The view changes month by month, so go soon.
ogm.s: ANSA (Feb 2025); Torino Oggi (Jan 2026). Map pin approximate

p: A bunker 18 m deep inside Le Nuove, the 19th-century prison, reached on a guided tour that also takes you through the cell blocks above. The story is told through the testimony of political and Jewish prisoners.
This is the best of Turin's shelters to actually visit: real depth and concrete, with the prison's radial wings on top.
Guided only, booking required (011 7604881, infoprenotazioni@museolenuove.it). Groups of 25, about 1 h 15. €8 (€5 reduced), free with the Abbonamento Musei.
A shelter 10 m under the courtyard of the town hall, built in 1940 for city staff: a single room 20 × 3 m for 50 people, with its original gas-tight doors and wall signs.

Free visits have been offered since 2017, and the master report mentions guided visits on the 4th Tuesday of the month for groups, booked through the Cerimoniale office. I could not find the current schedule.

visitazione.t: Mirafiori shelter and Chiesa della Visitazione
p: A tour that starts at the vanished Savoy castle of Mirafiori, visits the Chiesa della Visitazione, a 1934 concrete church with a crypt, and ends in the shelter that protected the old village.
Run by Arte e Musei, about 90 minutes. No dates were bookable in October 2026, so watch arteemusei.com. Not wheelchair-accessible.
visitazione.s: Arte e Musei. Map pin approximate

p: A concrete sports arena in Parco Ruffini, built in 1959–61 by Annibale Vitellozzi for Italia '61. It is the Turin twin of his Palazzetto in Rome (designed with Nervi), and it was his favourite: he said he preferred it for its daring composition.

Renovated in 2004, it seats about 4,000 and is home to the city's basketball team; since 2019 it's officially the Palazzetto Gianni Asti. The outside is free to see in the park; inside only on match or event days.

mirafiori.t: Fiat Mirafiori: Palazzina and Corso Tazzoli
p: Fiat's Mirafiori plant: a 220 m office block clad in white stone (1937–39), and behind it a clinker-brick factory front almost a kilometre long on Corso Tazzoli. The site covers about 2 km², and only part of it still produces cars.

This was the heart of Italian labour history. Porta 5 is the gate of the 1970s–80s struggles. The great strikes of March 1943 started inside, in Officina 19, and the riot of 3 July 1969 broke out on Corso Traiano by Gate 2. None of these spots has a plaque.
Stellantis plans to reopen the office block as a campus by 2027, so expect scaffolding. Private: look from the pavement. San Luca Evangelista is nearby.

socrem.t: Tempio Crematorio and Luogo del Ricordo
p: Turin's crematorium of 1882, the second in Italy, with a modern garden of grassy slopes and symbolic sculptures by Riccardo Cordero. Next door is the city's Luogo del Ricordo, where ashes are scattered among three fountains over rock gardens of Luserna stone and carried into the ground by the water.
It is central Turin's only modern landscape treatment of death, and a counterpart to the Cimitero Parco. Open in cemetery hours, free.
Turin's courthouse: a 300 m building of brick and about 30,000 m² of mirrored glass, built in 1990–2000. Megastructure scale, but not concrete brutalism. A pass-by only; the architect is disputed.

A church built entirely from standard factory-shed parts: 24 m concrete trusses, translucent U-glass walls, and one 24 × 84 m roof covering church, rectory and portico. On the forecourt stands a giant precast concrete cross. Gabetti and Isola built it in 1969–73 for workers at Fiat's Rivalta plant.

It is called one of the best-known Italian churches of the 1970s, and the architects themselves said it was "at the limit of poverty". In 1986–87 the trusses were painted with apostles, which the national census calls ill-advised.
Active parish; open around Mass times. Pair it with Collegno.

A pentagonal church where six exposed pillars carry a roof broken into triangles, and the light comes in through the gaps between them. It's by Nicola Mosso and a direct sibling of his Redentore; the national census rates it a work of excellence.
Mid-1960s, exact years unconfirmed; the concrete is partly clad in brick. Active parish.

Nichelino's big new church of 1970–73: three aisles under exposed concrete beams that cross upwards into a net, modelled on Mosso's Redentore. It has a concrete frame, brick and large windows, and seats over 600.
The parish reports roof leaks and decaying concrete. The building faces Piazza della Libertà (parish address Via Stupinigi 16); check the pin on satellite view.
nichelino.s: Diocese of Turin; nichelino.com. Map pin approximate

p: Oscar Niemeyer in Turin. The FATA headquarters at Pianezza is a 100 m office block hung from great arches, so it reads like a bridge on dry land: cantilevers of 21.30 m on each side, six hollow piers, and the middle floors suspended on steel ties.
Niemeyer designed it with the engineer Riccardo Morandi in 1976–79; it is the Turin sibling of his Mondadori headquarters near Milan. The census describes its "astonishing effect of suspension".

It is still FATA's offices at Via dei Prati 2: photograph it from the road and car-park edge, don't enter the grounds. After Niemeyer's Paris buildings, this is the most important pin on the Turin map.

A 17th-century charterhouse with a Juvarra gateway that became the Royal Asylum in 1852. At its peak it had 20 pavilions and its own internal railway. The walls came down after 1978, and the grounds are now a 40-hectare park, with some pavilions still abandoned.
The park is open daily. Local volunteer guides (Ciceroni Collegnesi) give free tours. The abandoned pavilions are fenced; don't go in. Pair with Piossasco.
The wine museum in the 18th-century cellars of the first Martini & Rossi plant (1864) at Pessione, under 30 km from Turin, with old stills and presses. Plant tours are also offered.
Online booking required; older listings give €9 (€6 reduced).
A sled-lift station built by Carlo Mollino at 2,286 m above Sauze d'Oulx in 1946–47, where Alpine farmhouse meets modernist structure. Sleds were hauled up the slope to it.
It was abandoned after the line became a ski lift in 1964, then restored in 1999–2005. Today it's a refuge restaurant in the ski season.
In summer walk up from Pian della Rocca via Sportinia; in winter take the lifts. Check the season opening with the municipality (0122 858009).
lagonero.s: MiC Atlante; Comune di Sauze d'Oulx. Map pin approximate

p: A chain of forts climbing the mountainside above Val Chisone, billed as the longest fortification in Europe. A covered staircase links the levels up the slope.

Visits are guided only, booked by phone. Routes take about 1, 3 or 7 hours; the long "Passeggiata Reale" costs €20. Autumn and winter hours are reported as Mon and Thu–Sun 10–17; another listing says 9–17, so confirm.
A fortress over the Val di Susa, rebuilt to its present form around 1830, with galleries, a great moat and underground passages. Visible from the road and the railway.
The 2026 season ran 20 June–27 September (€5, guided €8); otherwise it's closed until summer 2027.
A massive concrete gravity dam in Gran Paradiso National Park: 52 m high with a 302 m crest, inaugurated in 1931. It holds over 34 million m³ of water for the Orco valley power system.
Above 2,000 m on the Nivolet road are the Serrù (1951) and Agnel dams, and down the valley the Rosone power station, which Iren says produces about 720 GWh a year from the whole chain.
The dam is visible all year. The high road is closed in winter, so Serrù and Agnel are a summer trip. Interior visits only at Iren events.
ceresole.s: Iren; Unione Montana Gran Paradiso. Map pin approximate

moncenisio.t: Mont-Cenis: dam and Vallo Alpino forts
p: A huge earth-and-rock dam across the Mont-Cenis pass, 1.4 km long and 120 m high, billed as France's largest rockfill dam. Around it are the concrete strongpoints of Mussolini's Vallo Alpino (1933–42): cave works, firing posts and steel cupolas.
The plateau has been French since 1947. The forts are open but entered entirely at your own risk; bring a torch, stay on paths and treat interiors as unsafe. Start from Piana delle Fontanette.
The pass is closed in winter, so this is a summer trip.
moncenisio.s: SIOUH; Structurae; Vallo Alpino guides. Map pin approximate

stura.t: Valle Stura Vallo Alpino and Vinadio
p: Vallo Alpino forts in the Valle Stura near Cuneo: Opera 5 "San Membotto", one of the largest, with the only mortar block on the western Alps, plus works and barracks along the trails. The Forte di Vinadio runs a guided route into a 19th-century fort turned 20th-century command cave.
Well outside the Turin area: a long day trip.
stura.s: Unione Montana Valle Stura. Map pin approximate

p: An 1878 wool mill in the Biella hills that closed in 1964, sat empty for 20 years and was revived in 1984. It keeps its water-power transmission, period machinery and about 2 km of industrial archives, on the "Wool Road".
