Open summer Sundays (June–October) 14:30–18:30, €5; after October by appointment only (351 3902199). In autumn there is a night walk along the workers' paths.
pray.s: Fabbrica della Ruota / DocBi. Map pin approximate

p: Look closely at the bronze reliefs on the base of the equestrian statue in the middle of Piazza San Carlo. On the panel showing the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis there is a small dent: a bullet mark from the night of 22 September 1864, when soldiers fired into a crowd in this square. Almost nobody notices it.

Turin was protesting the decision to move Italy's capital to Florence. On 21 September cadets fired on demonstrators in Piazza Castello, and the next night here. The government fell within a week. It has been called the first state massacre of united Italy.
A plaque placed by the city in 1999 on the arcade pillar at no. 161 gives 52 dead and 187 wounded; later counts give between 55 and 62 dead. The city lays a wreath every 21 September.
It is Turin's closest equivalent to the bullet holes of Athens. The 2017 plaque and the brass bull are in the same square.

A bronze priest holding out a crucifix to a condemned man, standing on a traffic island at a busy junction. This is Saint Giuseppe Cafasso, the "gallows priest", and the statue stands on the exact spot where Turin's public gallows stood from 1835 to the early 1850s. The roundabout is still called the Rondò della Forca, the gallows roundabout.

Cafasso accompanied 57 condemned men to their deaths. The 1960 statue by Virgilio Audagna was requested by Italy's prisoners. Before this spot, hangings were held in Via Giulio, Piazza delle Erbe and Piazza San Carlo. Sources disagree on when they stopped here: 1852–53, or as late as 1863–64.

Turin's last hangman, Piero Pantoni, is said to have lived at Via Bonelli 2 with a wife who never went out for shame; that comes only from a blog and popular rumour. The "black magic triangle" stories are tourist esoterica.
The Museo Diffuso and the Arsenale plaque are within 600 m, making this the densest cluster of memory sites on the map.

A pleasant square with Cavour's statue in the middle, and no marker of any kind. Under French rule (1798–1814) it was renamed Place de la Liberté, and the guillotine stood roughly where Cavour now stands. 423 executions are reported for 1800–1814.

It was also the core of the old Jewish ghetto, and you can still see it in the buildings. The corner building at Via des Ambrois has four floors plus a mezzanine in the height where its neighbours have two or three: the crowding of the ghetto, written into a façade.

At no. 15, now an NH hotel, a 1957 plaque says "Here Antonio Gramsci lived in the years 1919–21", the years of *L'Ordine Nuovo* and the factory councils. The Fondazione Gramsci has display windows on the façade.
carlina.s: Istoreto; Atlante di Torino; ANPI MEMO. Map pin approximate

p: A small rifle range at the corner of Corso Svizzera, the only surviving part of a larger complex. Between 1943 and 1945 the Fascist Republic's firing squads shot around sixty partisans here. Inside there is a stone post on the parapet and a plaque with 59 names and their professions.

On 5 April 1944 eight members of the first Piedmont military committee of the Resistance were shot here, among them General Giuseppe Perotti; a plaque to four of them is on Via Luini 90. The exact count of victims differs: 59, "over 60", or 61. The first plaque was unveiled on 8 July 1945.
A ceremony is held every year in early April. Access times aren't confirmed, so check with the Museo Diffuso.

A granite monument on the road up to the Colle della Maddalena. On 2 April 1944, 27 prisoners from Le Nuove were brought here, shot together and buried in a common grave. On the back, the first small municipal plaque still shows the uncertainty about who some of the dead were.
They were exhumed on 27 May 1945. A plaque in Via Gramegna 11, put up by a group of neighbourhood friends for five of their own killed here, is a rare memorial made by people rather than the state.
Outdoors and always open; you need a car or bus. Commemoration every 2 April.
A street plaque that begins "in this place the Nazi-Fascist lead cut short…". It marks the exact spot where nine partisans, two of them unidentified Frenchmen, were shot on 12 October 1944.
Turin has hundreds of these "in questo luogo" plaques. Another, for nine shot in the square, is on Piazza Statuto, and the 1922 plaque in Piazza XVIII Dicembre is about 300 m away.
cibrario1.s: ANPI MEMO; Atlante delle stragi. Map pin approximate

p: A plaque on the corner of Via Cernaia, opposite the old Porta Susa station, for the "Turin massacre" of 18–20 December 1922. In three days the Fascist squads of Piero Brandimarte killed 11 people, among them the communist councillor Carlo Berruti, burned the Camera del Lavoro and wrecked the offices of *L'Ordine Nuovo*.

It was Italy's first big squadrist killing spree, two months after the March on Rome. The square took the date as its name in 1946. Brandimarte was convicted in 1950 and acquitted on appeal in 1952. A second plaque is in the metro station's north entrance; there is a ceremony every 18 December.
xviiidic.s: MuseoTorino; Consiglio Regionale; Il Caffè Torinese. Map pin approximate

p: A plaque on Via Po 46 for Roberto Crescenzio, a 22-year-old student. On 1 October 1977 masked militants who had split off from a far-left march threw Molotovs into the Angelo Azzurro bar, wrongly believing it was a neo-fascist hangout. He died two days later.
Four people were convicted. The plaque was unveiled in 2017. The place is a bar again today; the plaque is the point, not the venue.
A private doorway on Corso Re Umberto where, on 16 November 1977, the Red Brigades shot Carlo Casalegno, deputy editor of La Stampa. He died two weeks later, the first journalist killed by the BR.
Nothing on the street recalls it; his son has written about that absence. The only plaque is inside the La Stampa building. This is a spot, not a sight.
casalegno.s: Andrea Casalegno, Anni spietati. Map pin approximate

micca.t: Pietro Micca museum and siege tunnels
p: A museum of the 1706 siege, and below it the real thing: you go down to 6 and 14 m into the counter-mine tunnels the defenders dug under the citadel, to the stair Pietro Micca ran down and the spot where his body was found. This is the most physical site of its kind in Turin.

On the night of 29–30 August 1706 French troops broke into a gallery. Micca, a miner, lit a short fuse to blow it up and could not get clear. The original network ran about 21 km; you see about 400 m. The "Pietro Micca stair" was found bricked up in 1958 by Captain Guido Amoretti. The 1961 museum building stands where a French battery shelled the citadel.
Open Tue–Sun 10–18 (last entry 17). The tunnels must be booked (011 01167580) and run at 10:30, 14:30 and 16:30, plus 15:30 on Sundays. Cheap, and the Abbonamento Musei is valid.
A plaque to the siege dead is round the corner at Via Amoretti 7/A, where flowers are laid every 5 September. The Mastio is a few minutes away.

The keep of the 1564 pentagonal citadel, the only piece left of the fortress that held out in the siege of 1706. Cannons stand outside. Look at its front entrance: it's a fake door, and the grimacing mask on the keystone is said to be there to mock invaders.

Since 1896 it has housed the national artillery museum and now hosts exhibitions; in 2026 it opened a new underground archaeological area. Hours are irregular, so check before going; the outside is always visible.

The perimeter walls and part of the foyer of a theatre, open to the sky on Via Verdi. The 1857 theatre, relaunched by Riccardo Gualino in 1925, was gutted by bombs on 8 December 1942. The Resistance institute calls it the only conspicuous visible memory of the war damage in the city.
Across the street, the RAI centre at Via Verdi 16 was a barracks hit in August 1943; no scars are visible there today. Look from the street; no entry.

valdofusi.t: Piazza Valdo Fusi: the bombing void
p: An open square over an underground car park. Before the bombs, a full city block stood here, including the old Politecnico. The emptiness itself is the war scar.
On Via Po, at nos. 42–44, postwar buildings fill a bomb gap inside the 18th-century arcades. The Ex Borsa and Palazzo degli Affari face this square.
valdofusi.s: Boido & Davico (Politecnico, 2023); Istoreto. Map pin approximate

p: Turin's Moorish-style synagogue. The raid of 21 November 1942 gutted the interior and left only its four towers standing; it was rebuilt after the war. Round the side on Via Sant'Anselmo, the old "brides' door" at no. 7 is bricked up.

The story that people sifted gold from the rubble is, by the Resistance institute's own guide, a legend. The inside can be visited by booking with the Jewish Community. The walled door wasn't re-checked after 2020.
Eight tunnel mouths in the retaining wall below Monte dei Cappuccini, six of them bricked up and one widened and gated. This is one of only two public air-raid shelters dug into Turin's hill.
Inside are four cross-galleries lettered A to D, some now holding instruments of a space-physics institute. You can read it all from the pavement; no entry.
Four walled-up shelter entrances in Parco Leopardi, still marked "P.A.A." for Protezione Anti Aerea, the wartime civil defence. Public park; pin approximate.
A plaque on the arrivals side of Porta Nuova station, on Via Sacchi: "From this station the political deportees left for the Nazi extermination camps…". A one-minute stop when you pass the station.

Two brass "stumbling stones" in the pavement outside Via Po 25, for Michele Valabrega and Maria Irene Roscetti. They were arrested on 5 December 1943, deported on Primo Levi's convoy and murdered at Auschwitz. Their daughter Stella survived.

Turin has about 130 stones. At Piazza Castello 161 are the Colombo family, lured to a fake business meeting at a café on Via Roma and arrested by the SS. Others are at Corso San Maurizio 8 and Via San Domenico 0–1 (Father Girotti, who died at Dachau). The Museo Diffuso has walking routes linking them.
inciampo.s: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza. Map pin approximate

p: Two factory plaques moved into the Cascina Marchesa garden from the Fiat Grandi Motori plant. One marks where five worker-partisans fell under German tank fire on 27 April 1945, quoting Carducci: "and with stones one answers lead".
Public garden.
The courtyard of the Resistance museum holds plaques rescued from the Fiat Ferriere and Grandi Motori plants, recalling the factory that gave "the first spark of the revolt" of 18–28 April 1945.
Generally open in museum hours. The museum runs the shelter openings and the stumbling-stone walks.

supergacrash.t: Superga: the Grande Torino crash wall
p: Behind the basilica of Superga, the rear retaining wall still bears the mark of the impact of 4 May 1949, when the plane carrying the Grande Torino, then the best football team in Italy, crashed into the hill in fog. A marble plaque lists the victims.
All 31 on board died, including the whole squad. The site is under heritage protection, and in 2026 the city and Torino fans signed a pact to maintain it.
Free and always open on foot. Ride up on the Sassi–Superga rack tramway.
A working hotel on Piazza Carlo Felice. On 27 August 1950 Cesare Pavese was found dead in its room 346. No plaque outside, and the room is an ordinary guest room.
The hotel's own history notes it was hit by incendiary bombs on 8 December 1942. Caffè Elena is the place to sit where Pavese wrote.

An 1861 marble plaque on the corner of Via Lagrange and Via Cavour: Count Camillo di Cavour was born in this house on 10 August 1810 and died here on 6 June 1861, three months after Italy was proclaimed. His funeral was held in the church of the tiny piazzetta nearby.
Always visible. Del Cambio, where his table is kept, is a few minutes away.
cavourhouse.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: A small garden bed and a plaque in Largo Cibrario for the 64 people who died in the Cinema Statuto fire of 13 February 1983, most of them behind chained exits. The fire led directly to Italy's cinema fire-safety law.
The plaque was vandalised in 2017 and is still there. A second memorial is at the Cimitero Parco. The "evil vortex" stories online are nonsense: the fire was an accident.

An 1886 bronze plaque on the old arsenal, now Sermig's Arsenale della Pace. It honours Sergeant Paolo Sacchi, who on 26 April 1852 kept 40,000 kg of gunpowder from catching fire after the powder magazine exploded, and so "saved Turin".
The blast damaged every house in Borgo Dora. The death toll is disputed: 26, or 20 plus 3 who died in hospital. The story that Don Bosco's hat was blown off is tradition.

In April 1728 a 16-year-old Rousseau was registered here at the hospice for converts as "Rosso, Gio Giacomo, of Geneva, Calvinist", and abjured his faith a week or so later. He tells the story in the *Confessions*.

He later worked as a footman in Palazzo Solaro della Chiusa, now the MAO at Via San Domenico 11, where the "stolen ribbon" episode of the *Confessions* takes place. No plaque at either; the hospice building may not survive as such.
rousseau.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: A 7.94 m granite-and-bronze obelisk in the Piazza Statuto garden, topped with an armillary sphere. It isn't decoration: it was put up in 1808 on the stones that marked the Turin end of Giovanni Battista Beccaria's baseline, the line he measured to work out the size of the Earth. Its twin stands 11.8 km west at Rivoli, at the other end.

Beccaria measured the base in May 1760 for his *Gradus Taurinensis*, an attempt to find the length of one degree of meridian. He got 112.008 km (today's value is 111.139 km). He also noticed that the mass of the Alps was pulling his plumb line sideways. Napoleon's surveyors later built on his triangles. It is the closest thing Turin has to the standard-metre marks in Paris.

The stories about the 45th parallel or a "black magic" centre here are myth. Farmacia Almasio, on the corner of Via Manzoni 30 seconds away, has kept its furnishings of 1868 almost intact. The Frejus monument is at the other end of the square.

The western end of Beccaria's 1760 baseline: an obelisk identical to the one in Piazza Statuto, inaugurated on 8 October 1808, at the end of Corso Francia in Rivoli. Corso Francia runs almost along the measured line, so you can travel the whole base between the two.
Look also for a 1934 plaque set into the pavement by the newsstand at the start of Via Fratelli Piol. Beccaria extended the base up to Rivoli castle in 1762.
rivoliobelisk.s: Sena (Politecnico di Torino). Map pin approximate

p: Under the arcade on Via Po a plaque reads: "In the old chemical laboratory of this building, Ascanio Sobrero… first achieved the synthesis of nitroglycerine." This is where, in 1846–47, one of the most dangerous substances in chemistry was first made.

Sobrero noticed both its explosive power and its effect on blood vessels, which is why nitroglycerine is still used for angina. He was so frightened by it that he was dismayed when Alfred Nobel turned it into dynamite.
His monument in the Valentino, a bronze bust above a young titan tearing at rocks (1914), sits near the Borgo Medievale.

The former Ospizio di Carità on Via Po, where on 7 November 1896 Vittorio Calcina, the Lumière brothers' man in Italy, showed about twenty short films to an invited audience including the mayor. It is often called Italy's first public film screening; Rome disputes it with a screening in March 1896.

The room ran as the "Kinematografo Lumière" until March 1897, when the shows moved to a beer hall on Via Garibaldi. There is no plaque; you see the façade. Turin then became Italy's first film capital: see the Ambrosio and Itala studios.

The old university of 1714–20, with its arcaded courtyard on Via Po. Beccaria taught physics here from 1748. On the night of 25–26 January 1904 a fire burned five rooms of the National Library housed here, destroying much of its manuscript collection.

Donations came from all over the world. The chemist Icilio Guareschi, trying to save fused parchments, effectively founded the chemistry of library conservation. The courtyard is usually open on weekdays.
unipo.s: MuseoTorino; BNU Torino; RSUT (2019). Map pin approximate

p: Palazzo Madama's west tower was Turin's astronomical observatory from 1822 to 1912, with a rotating dome and, from 1885, a 30 cm refractor. The city's new electric lights ruined the sky, and the observatory moved out to Pino Torinese. The dome was demolished in 1920; only the tower remains.
An earlier observatory stood on the roof of the Academy of Sciences from 1790. Nothing survives of either, so this is a look-up-and-imagine stop.

A two-storey office block on the Dora and behind it a glass-roofed stage of 50 × 25 m on iron pillars: the studio of Ambrosio Film, Italy's biggest silent-film company. Pietro Fenoglio built it in 1911–13, and the façade is unchanged.

Ambrosio, founded in 1906–07, employed over 75 actors and 400 staff. In the First World War it made aircraft propellers, and it went bankrupt in 1924. The building is now Teatro Espace and a café. Its earlier 1909 stage was round the corner at Via Catania 30.
The site of Itala Film, where Giovanni Pastrone made *Cabiria* (1914), the epic that taught Hollywood the travelling shot. The studios were built here in 1906–15.
Whether any building survives is unconfirmed: a look-from-the-street stop only.
itala.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: A working three-screen cinema inside the 1870s glass arcade of the Galleria Subalpina. A Lumière projection room opened in the basement in 1905.

The cinema calls itself Italy's first art-house cinema; that's disputed (art-house programming started in 1971). A good place to actually see a film. The Nietzsche plaque is at the other end of the arcade.
romano.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: Fiat's first factory, built in 1899–1900 on Corso Dante. During the "red two years", in September 1920, it was a centre of the factory occupations, when workers took over the plants for a month. It was bombed on 8 December 1942 and is now lofts.
No plaque. The founding deed was signed at Palazzo Bricherasio; the company later moved to the Lingotto and Mirafiori.

The palace where Fiat's founding deed was signed in July 1899 (the date is disputed, 1 or 11 July). Outside, the only plaque is for the poet Berchet; inside hangs a copy of Delleani's painting of the signing.
It's now a bank, so outside only except during events.
bricherasio.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: Under the arcades at Piazza Castello and Via Viotti, a plaque says that in 1786 Antonio Benedetto Carpano created his vermouth "in this house". His shop here is documented; that he invented vermouth is tradition.
Check the plaque in person; its date is unknown. To drink one in context, go to Caffè Elena, where he is said to have refined it.

A public bench painted black and white, with a plaque, at Corso Re Umberto and Corso Vittorio Emanuele II. Juventus was founded on a bench here in 1897 by school students. This one is a stand-in, repainted in July 2025 and placed opposite the original spot.
The real bench has been in the J Museum since 2012. The first club meetings were held in the Canfari brothers' workshop at Corso Re Umberto 42.
juvebench.s: Torino Cronaca; Juventus. Map pin approximate

p: Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine of this bar, then the Birreria Voigt, on 3 December 1906, by members of Football Club Torinese and Juventus dissidents led by Alfred Dick. A plaque and the founders' photo are inside.
Have a drink where the derby began. The team's tragic end is at Superga.
norman.s: Torino FC history. Map pin approximate

p: A lone chimney in Parco Dora, from the stamping shops of Michelin's first Italian plant (1906). It's all that's left. Botta's church, with its own kept chimney, is nearby. Public park.
michelin.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: A faded plaque, hard to read: "Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange was born in this house on 25 January 1736." The mathematician later chaired the commission that created the metric system in France.
His statue (1867) stands nearby in Piazza Lagrange. He was also a founder of the Academy of Sciences.

Three 19th-century museums in one university building: Luigi Rolando's anatomy rooms with their old cases, wax and papier-mâché models; Cesare Lombroso's museum of criminal anthropology, with skulls, crime objects and inmates' art; and Garnier Valletti's hundreds of artificial fruits.

Lombroso claimed criminals could be recognised by their skulls. His science is long discredited, and that is why the museum matters: it shows how a theory can dress prejudice up as fact. The anatomy museum was founded in 1739; its rooms cover about 900 m².
Open Mon–Sat 10–18 (last entry 17:30). Three-museum ticket €10 (€6 reduced). The fruit museum's entrance is on Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 52.
anatomici.s: Museo di Anatomia Umana; Abbonamento Musei

p: A pharmacy trading since 1667, with 18th-century wooden fittings, its original jars and a bronze mortar dated 1718. Step in during shop hours: it's still a working pharmacy, so buy something small.
A pharmacy in the same family since 1682, with a big historic sign and its original fittings. Shop hours.
Nearby, the Farmacia della Consolata (Via delle Orfane 25) has fittings MuseoTorino calls unique; its "since 1510" is marketing.

A 1949 plaque signed "Turin remembers" on Via dell'Arcivescovado 7. The building held the Piedmont edition of the socialist *Avanti!* and the rooms where Gramsci's *L'Ordine Nuovo* was written. Later it held Einaudi's first offices.
Gramsci's lodging plaque is on Piazza Carlina.
ordinenuovo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

teatronuovo.t: Teatro Nuovo: the march of the 40,000
p: On 14 October 1980, day 35 of the strike that had blocked Fiat, a meeting of supervisors here overflowed into a silent march to the city hall: the "march of the 40,000". It ended the strike and became a turning point for the unions in Turin.
Crowd estimates range from 12,000 to 40,000. There is no plaque.
teatronuovo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: The buildings of an asbestos factory that ran from 1911 to 1952, listed in a 1984 census as "of documentary interest". Its current state is unconfirmed; outside only.
An IEEE Milestone plaque for Galileo Ferraris, who discovered the rotating magnetic field in 1885, the principle behind most electric motors. It was dedicated in 2021.

Where it is now is unclear. IEEE lists the Energy Center (Via Borsellino 38/16, entrance hall), but a 2024 Politecnico release puts it with a new bust in the atrium of Sala "Emma Strada" on the main campus. Check both.
ferraris.s: IEEE / ETHW; Politecnico di Torino (2024). Map pin approximate

p: Luigi Lavazza's grocery of 1895, where he started blending coffee. It's now the "San Tommaso 10" café and restaurant, with company-history photos on the walls. Have an espresso where it started.
lavazza.s: Lavazza; Michelin guide. Map pin approximate

p: The corner of Via Ormea and Via Donizetti, where Vincenzo Lancia founded his company on 27 November 1906. A 1907 fire destroyed the first prototype, and the doors are said to have been widened to get the first car out.
No plaque: a spot only.

Still a working airfield. On 22 May 1917 Mario De Bernardi took off from the Pomilio company field here for Rome in a Pomilio PC1, carrying 200 kg of mail with specially overprinted stamps: the world's first airmail stamp.

The field is now the Aero Club Torino's, and Leonardo's aircraft division is still on Corso Francia. Turin's first aerodrome, at Mirafiori (now Parco Colonnetti), was one of Italy's biggest early flying schools.
The university's botanic garden, a royal garden of 1729 next to the Valentino castle, with an old Ginkgo, cedar and yew in its Boschetto. A new railing lets passers-by see in.
Open late March to mid-November, Sat 14:30–19, Sun 10–19 (2025 schedule), €5. Closed for the season from about 17 November.
ortobot.s: Turismo Torino; Artribune. Map pin approximate

p: The regional natural science museum, in the former San Giovanni hospital. It closed after an explosion in August 2013 and partly reopened in January 2024; more works were approved in October 2026, so check what's open.
scienzenat.s: Regione Piemonte; mentelocale (Jan 2026). Map pin approximate

p: Corso Re Umberto 75: Primo Levi was born and died in this house, and his surname is still on the doorbell. A plaque is not confirmed. A spot to stop, not a sight.
Rita Levi-Montalcini ran her secret bedroom laboratory on the same street in 1940 (number unknown). The Primo Levi study centre is in Via del Carmine.
primolevi.s: The Spectator; studenti.it. Map pin approximate

p: A workers' mutual-aid society that still meets, one of Turin's old SOMS clubs, with banners, members' photos and old documents on the walls. These clubs were the welfare system of the working class before the state had one.
Go in as a guest of the bar, if it's open.
soms.s: Gambero Rosso (Jul 2026); Regione Piemonte. Map pin approximate

p: A little Liberty-era urinal kiosk in front of the pharmacy on Piazza Villari, cast in "artificial stone" and stamped "U. Renzi". It is one of the two oldest survivors of Turin's historic public urinals, and since 2023–24 it has been painted in pastel green and pink as a street-art piece.

In the 1870s–80s the hygienist Giacinto Pacchiotti campaigned for Paris-style urinals. The Turin firm of Umberto Renzi moved from iron kiosks to cast stone, and its curved 1930s "Modello '900" spread across Italy and its colonies. About 29 Renzi urinals survive among the city's 190 public toilets; the city wants to keep 13 as historic objects, and others are being demolished one by one.

Mostly locked or tagged: things to look at, not to use. Others on the map: Piazza Sassari (the other Liberty one), Corso Regina Margherita 103 and Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 16. More at Corso Maroncelli 18, Parco Michelotti and the military hospital on Corso IV Novembre.
The other Liberty-style Renzi urinal: a pierced kiosk on little columns near Via Cigna. With Piazza Villari it is one of the two oldest. Condition not re-checked in 2026.
A classic 1930s Renzi "Modello '900" urinal, the curved kiosk that spread across Italy, in front of Corso Regina Margherita 103 near the Giardini Reali. Tagged, but intact.
Another Renzi "Modello '900" kiosk, on the side road in front of Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 16, just before the Teatro Nuovo.

A modest Liberty building of 1901 at the corner of Via Vanchiglia that still does the job it was built for: public baths, where people without a bathroom at home come for a shower. Volunteers from the Alpini civil protection run it, and it had 7,478 visits in 2022.

Turin built these baths after the 1908 town plan, mostly to designs by the city engineer Camillo Dolza, for workers' housing without bathrooms. This one was lightly damaged in July 1943 and keeps its original structure and function.
Other baths on the map: Via Morgari (the prettiest, now a café), San Donato (a library), Via Agliè and Via Cherasco (still working).

Camillo Dolza's Liberty bathhouse in San Salvario, with curving low wings and a cornice of alternating frogs and shells. Built in 1900–1910 so locals could wash, it's now the Casa del Quartiere: a café and community centre.
The best of Turin's public baths to sit in. Have a coffee and look up at the frogs.
The first shower baths of Borgo San Donato (1900, later 40 tubs), with a wash-house decorated with animals and the custodian's house. It's now the Gabriele d'Annunzio library.
A working 1956 municipal bathhouse in Barriera di Milano. It replaced baths housed in an old toll house on Piazza Crispi, demolished in 1959.
It closed in 1990, reopened in 2005, and is now a Casa del Quartiere with an active programme.
An early-20th-century bathhouse in Nizza Millefonti, nicknamed "Barrito", where eight showers on the first floor still run for the public.

A low yellow building on Piazza Rebaudengo: the customs office of 1912, at the main northern goods entry into the city, still in its original form. It now houses a family centre and carries a 2017 mural of a flying ship by Alessandra Carloni.

Until 1930 goods entering Turin paid a duty at a walled line. The 1912 wall ran 23 km, and its gates stood on big regular squares like this one, which is why they exist at all. The yellow colour is the giveaway.

Other survivors: Piazza Stampalia 3 (Barriera di Lanzo), Piazza Cirene (Barriera di Pianezza) and Piazza Bengasi (Barriera di Nizza, restored 2023). One source says a post of the older 1853 wall survives at Corso Moncalieri 80.
The 1912 toll staff quarters of the Barriera di Lanzo, built to the standard design and later enlarged. Now a district meeting centre. One of the four survivors of the customs wall.

The 1912 customs house on the Turin–Moncalieri border. It was nearly demolished for Metro 1, then restored by 2023 with a new roof and the façade repainted in its original colours. Street-art panels were added when Bengasi station opened.
bengasi.s: MuseoTorino; Torino Oggi (2023). Map pin approximate

p: Inside the Mercato Centrale, Fuksas's glass market hall at Porta Palazzo, two round 19th-century ice chambers are left open to view in a sunken plaza. You see their brick domes, sloping floors for meltwater and the hatches where ice was dropped in from above.

They were found in 2002 while the hall was being built. Maps from 1753 already show icehouses here, between Porta Palazzo and the Consolata, filled with ice cut from Dora channels in winter. The street name Strada delle Ghiacciaie recalls the trade.
Under Piazza Emanuele Filiberto, the 1845 Panizza icehouses at Via delle Orfane 32 spiral down about four levels and are still used by market vendors to store barrows; they're not open to the public.
The Mercato Centrale is free to enter in opening hours; the ground floor has been reorganised more than once, so check.

A column by the Borgo Medievale entrance in the Valentino, marked with the heights reached by the Po's great floods. The highest is October 1839, at 6.20 m. The floods of 2000 and 2016 came within 30–50 cm of it.

On 4 May 1949, the day of the Superga crash, the river rose to its fourth-highest mark. Stand next to it and look up: that is where the river was. It is the only flood marker in the city; none was found on the Murazzi.

A small museum of washerwomen in the parish courtyard of Bertolla, Turin's laundry village from about 1872 to the 1960s. Three rooms of washing tools, including the "scagn" kneeling board, photos and costumes.
A 1935 ban on drying laundry along the city's rivers is part of the story. Free, by appointment only (349 872 2649 in older sources).

A rack tramway that climbs 3.1 km from Sassi up to the basilica of Superga, at gradients of up to 21%, in cars from 1934. Locals call it the Dentiera, "the dentures", for its toothed rack. The ride takes about 18 minutes.

It opened in 1884 on Agudio's unusual cable system and was converted to an electric rack in 1935. GTT bills it as unique in Italy. Motor car D2 has been restored in its original livery (2026), and Sassi station keeps a small history room in near-original condition.

Reopened on 3 April 2026. The summer timetable runs hourly 10:00–18:00 from Sassi, with no service on Wednesdays (a bus replaces it). Winter suspensions happen, so check gtt.to.it. The Grande Torino crash wall is at the top.
A single, very flat stone arch over the Dora: 45 m span with only 5.5 m of rise. Ordered by Napoleon in 1807 and opened in 1830, it is called unique among Europe's early 19th-century stone bridges.

Legend says its engineer, Carlo Bernardo Mosca, sat in a boat under it when the scaffolding came down, to prove it would hold. It was named after him only in 1868. See it best from the riverside path. The old Torino–Ceres terminus is just north.
The 1869 terminus of the Lanzo Valleys railway on Corso Giulio Cesare, disused since June 1986. Outside only. Next to Ponte Mosca.

On the side wall of the cathedral facing the passage to the Piazzetta Reale, a vertical noon line marks the zodiac signs, Capricorn at the top and Cancer at the bottom, with a star-shaped hole as the gnomon. At solar noon the spot of light falls on the line.
Esoteric guides read it as an anti-Church code; a sundial specialist calls it a perfectly normal and correct meridian. Go around solar noon: about 12:20 in winter, 13:20 in summer.
Seven torèt, Turin's green cast-iron fountains with a bull's head spout, set in a semicircle on Via Stradella. The city has about 800 of them; the first was installed in 1862.

Other variants: the "lovers", two torèt facing each other at Via Stampatori 4, and a lioness-headed one in Parco della Pellerina. These rest on a single guide source. Press a finger on the spout and water comes out of a hole on top for drinking.

torobrass.t: Brass bull of Piazza San Carlo
p: A brass rearing bull set into the pavement of the western arcade of Piazza San Carlo, near Caffè Torino. Step on its testicles and spin round for luck; the wear tells you everyone does.

Under the Prefettura arcade, students rub the little finger of a bronze Columbus before exams for luck. The monument is actually Dino Somà's 1923 memorial to the Italians from Latin America who volunteered in the First World War; Columbus is only a medallion below the infantryman.
A historian called the ritual "a banal amulet". The finger is said to have been replaced from wear.
ditocolombo.s: Emilio Franzina; GuidaTorino. Map pin approximate

p: At the west end of Piazza Statuto, a fountain topped by a pyramid of real rocks dug out of the Frejus rail tunnel, with marble Titans and a winged bronze figure on top. It was inaugurated in 1879 to celebrate the tunnel's engineers, Sommeiller, Grandis and Grattoni.
The winged figure is the Genius of Science, not "Lucifer" as the black-magic tours claim. Its sculptor, Luigi Belli, later disowned the work. An inscription for the workers was only added in 1971.
frejus.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026

p: A carved door of 1675, made in Paris, on Palazzo Trucchi di Levaldigi, with a gilded devil's-head knocker held by two snakes. Turin calls it the "Devil's door".

The palace has been a bank since 1939; in 1738 a tarot-card factory was licensed here. The ghost stories have no evidence. On the same corner of Via XX Settembre and Via Alfieri look for the "Horns of Pan" mask, and more masks at the regional council entrance, Via Alfieri 15.

Turin's first skyscraper, 87 m of 1933–34 rationalist tower at the corner of Piazza Castello and Via Roma. It was meant to be the Fascist party headquarters, which is why locals called it "the Duce's finger".

The insurer Reale Mutua took it instead. It once carried an air-raid siren. From the little square with the news kiosk you can see where the design changed during building. The city's own plaque on it gives the wrong dates.

toro.t: T'oro: bull bursting from a wall
p: Half a bull with golden horns smashing out of a brick wall on Via delle Orfane, with a scarab nearby: *T'oro*, a pun on toro (bull) and oro (gold), by Richi Ferrero. The bull is Turin's emblem.
Ferrero also made the futurist gate at Via Lagrange 12, showing a motorbike's movement in wrought iron (visible when the courtyard is open).
toro.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: In the courtyard passage of Palazzo Villa, between Piazza San Carlo and Via Lagrange, a big red head of David hangs upside down: Andrea Salvatori's play on Kant, "the starry sky within me, the moral law above me". Look up as you walk through.
david.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: An iron bench in the Valentino's rock garden where two street lamps sit side by side, one leaning on the other, with a cat: Rodolfo Marasciuolo's "lamps in love" (2002). Still there in February 2026.
lampioni.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: The central section of a real submarine, sitting in the Valentino park by the river. The *Andrea Provana* was a training submarine of 1915–18; after an accidental explosion in 1927 its middle section was shown at the 1928 Expo and placed here in 1933.
Only one guide source describes it, so check it's still there.
Look up at Via Madama Cristina 19: two large stone bats hang under the third-floor balconies of this 1876 building. Single source; pin approximate.

A square of about 17 × 13 m, with its own street sign and house number, at the corner of Via Cavour and Via Carlo Alberto. It was left over when the church was remodelled in 1901, and Cavour's funeral was held in that church in 1861.
It is often called the smallest square in Italy; that's disputed, and the city treats it as part of the neighbouring piazzetta. Cavour's birth-and-death house is a minute away.
piazzetta.s: TorinoToday; Piemonte Go. Map pin approximate

p: Via Ercole Ricotti, between Corso Regina Margherita and Lungo Dora Siena, is Turin's shortest street: 23–30 m, with only two house numbers on two mirror-image buildings.
The narrowest street, vicolo Santa Maria in the Quadrilatero, is 2.85 m. The longest is Corso Regina Margherita (about 7.7 km), the widest Corso Salvemini (127.5 m).
ricotti.s: Atlante di Torino. Map pin approximate

p: Nothing to see, but stand here: the city's civic tower rose on this corner from 1379 to 1801, with a gilded bull on its spire and Turin's first public clock (1387). It was demolished on 10 May 1801 to straighten Via Garibaldi.
An old source says part of its east wall survives in Via Genova; unverified.

routes.name: Quadrilatero and Porta Palazzo: cannonballs, ice-houses and the arsenal
routes.when: The Mercato Centrale is closed on Mondays and Sundays; Al Bicerin closes on Wednesdays.
routes.summary: The town-hall shelter, the lost civic tower, the pierced palazzo, Lavazza's first shop, the Duomo meridian, Rousseau's church, a 1682 pharmacy, the bull in the wall, the 1706 cannonballs, a bicerin, the ice-houses under the market, the arsenal plaque, Ponte Mosca and the old Ceres terminus. About 3 km.

routes.name: Piazza Castello to Carignano: Mollino's Regio, Nietzsche and the first parliament
routes.when: Royal Library and Accademia library close at weekends or Sunday. Regio backstage tours Sat 15:00/16:30 and Sun 11:00, booked online.
routes.summary: The Royal Library, Columbus's finger, the Regio, Palazzo Madama's lost observatory, the tramezzino café, Cinema Romano, Carpano's vermouth, the Torre Littoria, the Torino FC bar, Cavour's table, the first parliament, Nietzsche's lodging, Palazzo Campana and the Accademia. About 2 km.

routes.name: Piazza San Carlo and south: the 1864 bullet, Cavour's house and Mollino's offices
routes.when: Daytime; the Masino pharmacy keeps shop hours. Everything else is street-side.
routes.summary: A 1667 pharmacy, the upside-down David, the lucky bull, the bullet dent and the 2017 plaque, the patriots' café, the devil's door, L'Ordine Nuovo, Lagrange's and Cavour's houses, the Fiat founding palace, the smallest piazzetta, Mollino's Palazzo degli Affari, the Borsa and the Valdo Fusi bomb void. About 2.5 km.

routes.name: Via Po and Vanchiglia: nitroglycerine, the Lumière show and the bombed theatre
routes.when: The old university courtyard is open on weekdays. Caffè Elena closes on Wednesdays. Ambrosio is a longer walk out along the Dora.
routes.summary: Caffè Fiorio, the old university, pietre d'inciampo, Sobrero's lab, the 1896 Lumière screening, the Angelo Azzurro plaque, the ruined Teatro di Torino, Palazzo Nuovo, the guillotine square, Pavese's café, the Fetta di Polenta, a Renzi urinal, the shortest street, the working 1901 baths and the Ambrosio film studios. About 5 km.

routes.name: Cittadella, Statuto and San Donato: siege tunnels, the Frejus pyramid and Beccaria's baseline
routes.when: Pietro Micca tunnels Tue–Sun, booked (10:30, 14:30, 16:30). Le Nuove shelter guided only, booked (011 7604881).
routes.summary: The Cittadella keep, the 1706 counter-mine tunnels, the 1922 massacre plaque, the Museo Diffuso's factory plaques, the gallows square, the Frejus monument, Beccaria's obelisk, the BBPR tower, the 1944 Via Cibrario killings, the San Donato baths and the Cinema Statuto memorial; optional Le Nuove prison shelter, the courthouse and Ferraris's IEEE plaque. About 3 km.

routes.name: Porta Nuova and San Salvario: Pavese, Primo Levi, the synagogue and Lombroso
routes.when: Lombroso and the anatomy museums Mon–Sat 10–18. Caffè Platti reopened 23 Oct 2026.
routes.summary: Caffè Platti, the Juventus bench, Pavese's hotel, the deportation plaque, Casalegno's doorway, Primo Levi's house, the natural-sciences museum, the synagogue's walled door, the palace of bats, Lancia's first workshop, the frog-and-shell bathhouse and the Lombroso and anatomy museums. About 5 km.

routes.name: Valentino and Borgo Po: flood column, a submarine, Nervi's hall and Neoliberty
routes.when: Botanic garden weekends only, to mid-November. Torino Esposizioni reopens as the central library on 11 Dec 2026.
routes.summary: Nervi's Torino Esposizioni, the Po flood column, the lamp-post bench, the botanic garden, a Renzi urinal, the Provana submarine, the Teatro Nuovo of the 1980 march, then over the river to the Casa dell'Obelisco, the Parco Leopardi and Cappuccini shelter mouths, a mutual-aid club and the Itala Film site. About 5 km.

routes.name: Lingotto and Italia '61: Fiat's first plant, the rooftop track and the monorail stumps
routes.when: Pista 500 is closed on Mondays. Metro to Lingotto. Moriondo and Nichelino are a bus or car hop south.
routes.summary: The OSI-Ghia ruins, Fiat's first plant, the working Via Cherasco baths, the Lingotto rooftop track, the Olympic arch, the monorail station, fountain and viaduct stumps, the Bengasi toll house and Nervi and Ponti's abandoned hall; optional Mosso's Moriondo church and the Nichelino net-roof church. About 8 km.

routes.name: San Paolo and Mirafiori: Vitellozzi, Jaretti & Luzi, the Fiat front and the park cemetery
routes.when: A bus day. Cimitero Parco open daily 8:30–17:30. The Mirafiori shelter tour has no dates now.
routes.summary: The asbestos factory, Bianco's San Francesco di Sales, Santa Teresa, the PalaRuffini, Torri Pitagora, Mosso's Redentore, the 1 km Fiat Mirafiori front, the Visitazione shelter, Roggero's San Luca and the 1972 park cemetery. About 14 km; buses help.

routes.name: North-west by bus: the shelter, the Martinetto, Parco Dora and the Vallette
routes.when: The Piazza Risorgimento shelter opens only on special dates (book 011 01120780). Santo Volto open daily 8–19.
routes.summary: The air-raid shelter under Piazza Risorgimento, the Martinetto firing range, the Michelin chimney, Botta's Santo Volto, the ex-Superga sneaker plant, the seven-torèt fountain, the Stampalia toll house, the Villari urinal, Bianco's San Paolo Apostolo and the Vallette estate; optional Santa Maria Goretti, the ThyssenKrupp sheds and the first-airmail airfield. About 10 km.

routes.name: North-east by bus: the crematorium, the Trincerone, the toll house and Falchera
routes.when: Crematorium garden in cemetery hours. Buses along Corso Vercelli and Corso Giulio Cesare.
routes.summary: The 1882 crematorium garden, Gesù Operaio, the Grandi Motori shells, the Via Agliè baths, the Sassari urinal, the Cascina Marchesa plaques, Corso Taranto's migrant slabs, the Trincerone before Metro 2, the 1912 Rebaudengo toll house, San Michele and Astengo's Falchera; optional laundry museum at Bertolla. About 12 km.

routes.name: The hill: the rack tram, the Grande Torino wall and Pian del Lot
routes.when: Tram hourly from Sassi 10–18 in season, no service Wednesdays; winter suspensions. Pian del Lot needs a car.
routes.summary: The 1884 Sassi–Superga rack tram, the basilica's rear wall still marked by the 1949 crash; optional Pian del Lot, where 27 prisoners were shot in 1944.

routes.name: West belt by car: the asylum park, Niemeyer's FATA and Piossasco
routes.when: A car day. FATA is weekday offices: view from the road. Piossasco church open around Mass.
routes.summary: The Collegno charterhouse-asylum park, Niemeyer and Morandi's 'land bridge' at Pianezza, Beccaria's twin obelisk at Rivoli and Gabetti & Isola's factory-shed church at Piossasco. About 30 km by road.

tours.name: Sieges, science and the guillotine: 18th-century Turin
tours.intro: In 1706 a French army besieged Turin; its shot is still in the walls and its tunnels under the Cittadella. The century that followed measured the meridian, opened the cafés and ended with a French guillotine in Piazza Carlina.
tours.how: On foot, west to east across the old centre. Book the Pietro Micca tunnels ahead.

stops.note: The 1564 keep, the only part of the Cittadella that held out in 1706 and still stands.
The counter-mine galleries where Pietro Micca fired the mine on the night of 29–30 August 1706.
Beccaria measured his geodetic baseline from here in 1760; the obelisk went up in 1808.
Open since 1763, opposite the Consolata.
Iron shot from 1706, and from the 1799 fighting over the Cittadella, walled in as memorials.
A pharmacy in the same family since 1682.
Trading since 1667; a bronze mortar of 1718.
The Academy of Sciences: its roof held Turin's first real observatory (1790); Lagrange was a founder.
Opened 1757, the oldest of the grand restaurants.
Guarini's baroque palace, later Italy's first parliament.
Founded 1780, the conservative café.
Under French rule (1798–1814) the guillotine stood here; 423 executions are reported.

story: The century opens with the siege of 1706: 117 days, a war fought partly underground in the counter-mine galleries, and Pietro Micca's mine. The shot fired into the city was later walled into façades as memorials.
Peace built a capital of science and cafés: Beccaria's meridian baseline (1760), the Academy of Sciences and its observatory, Del Cambio, Al Bicerin, Fiorio.
It closes with the French: from 1798 Piazza Carlina became the Place de la Liberté and its guillotine.

tours.name: Cavour's capital: the Risorgimento
tours.intro: Turin was Italy's first capital. From the gallows square to the hall where the Kingdom was proclaimed in 1861 and the night soldiers fired on the crowd in 1864.
tours.how: On foot from Valdocco to Piazza San Carlo; Al Bicerin closes on Wednesdays.

stops.note: Public hangings were held here 1835–1853; Cafasso accompanied 57 condemned men.
Cavour is said to have drunk here waiting for the royal family to leave the Consolata.
26 April 1852: the powder magazine blew up and Sergeant Sacchi kept 40,000 kg of powder from following.
Founded by Carlo Alberto in 1831–37.
Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo and Cavour were regulars; the Whist Club story is tradition.
The 1861 hall where the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed.
Cavour's table, marked with a plaque, facing the parliament.
The patriots' café, closed several times on suspicion of subversion.
22 September 1864: protests against moving the capital to Florence; the bullet dent is on the plinth.
Cavour was born and died in this house (1810, 1861).

story: Turin was the first capital of united Italy, proclaimed in 1861 in Palazzo Carignano. The men of unification lived within a few streets: Cavour's table at Del Cambio, the patriots at Caffè San Carlo, the conservatives at Fiorio.

The period had its violence: the gallows at the Rondò until 1853, the 1852 powder-magazine explosion in Borgo Dora, and on 21–22 September 1864 cadets firing on crowds protesting the move of the capital to Florence; the dent is still on the Caval ëd Bronz.

tours.name: Belle Époque: cinema, cars and public baths
tours.intro: Between the 1884 rack tram and the 1912 customs wall, Turin became Italy's film capital and its car city, and built public baths for workers' housing without bathrooms.
tours.how: A transit day: centre on foot, then tram and bus to the edges.

stops.note: 7 November 1896: the Lumière shorts, often called Italy's first public screening (Rome disputes it).
A Lumière room opened in this arcade's basement in 1905.
Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine on 3 December 1906.
Fiat's founding deed was signed here in July 1899.
Dolza's Liberty bathhouse, frogs and shells on the cornice.
Fiat's first plant, 1899–1900.
Lancia founded at this corner on 27 November 1906.
1901 baths, still working.
Fenoglio's 1911–13 studio for Italy's biggest silent-film company.
The chimney of Michelin's first Italian plant (1906).
The 1912 customs-wall toll house, original form.
The 1884 Sassi–Superga line, rack since 1935.

story: Turin lost the capital in 1865 and reinvented itself: by 1914 Ambrosio and Itala made it Italy's film capital, and Fiat (1899) and Lancia (1906) its car city.
The 1908 plan put public baths in the workers' districts; several still sell showers. In 1912 a new customs wall ringed the city, and its yellow toll houses still stand on the big 'barrier' squares.

tours.name: Fascism and the bombs
tours.intro: From the squads of 1922 to the raids of 1940–45: the massacre plaque, the Fascist tower, the shelters and the ruins the bombs left.
tours.how: Mostly on foot in the centre; the Piazza Risorgimento shelter is a tram ride and opens only on special dates.

stops.note: 18–20 December 1922: Brandimarte's squads killed 11 and burned the Camera del Lavoro.
A 1940 shelter for town-hall staff, original doors and signs.
The 1933–34 tower meant as the Fascist HQ, 'il dito del Duce'.
The former Casa del Littorio, where the Brigate Nere held partisans.
A whole block, the old Politecnico, bombed away.
Gutted on 8 December 1942: the city's only conspicuous visible war ruin.
Eight shelter mouths in the hill, six bricked up.
The 21 November 1942 raid gutted the interior; the towers survived.
One of the big public shelters, three concrete galleries 12 m down.

story: Fascism arrived in Turin with the December 1922 massacre. The regime left the Torre Littoria on Piazza Castello and the Casa del Littorio (now Palazzo Campana).
From June 1940 the city was bombed; only 15% of the population had a safe shelter. The Teatro di Torino ruin and the Valdo Fusi void are what remains to see above ground.

tours.name: Occupation and Resistance
tours.intro: September 1943 to April 1945: the prison, the firing range, the street executions, the deportations and the insurrection.
tours.how: Spread out: tram between the centre stops; Pian del Lot needs a car.

stops.note: Le Nuove held political and Jewish prisoners; its shelter is 18 m down.
About sixty partisans shot by RSI squads; 59 names on the plaque.
Nine partisans shot on this spot on 12 October 1944.
Factory plaques from the April 1945 insurrection.
Five worker-partisans fell here under tank fire on 27 April 1945.
The Valabrega stones: deported on Primo Levi's convoy.
Political deportees left from this station.
27 prisoners from Le Nuove shot on 2 April 1944.

story: After September 1943 Le Nuove filled with political and Jewish prisoners; the Martinetto range and Pian del Lot were where many were shot.
The city rose on 26–28 April 1945; workers' squads fought from the factories, and their plaques survive at Cascina Marchesa and the Museo Diffuso.

tours.name: The Fiat century: factory, migrants and boom
tours.intro: Fiat shaped Turin and drew migrants from the south. Follow it from the rooftop test track to Italia '61 and the housing, churches and cemetery the boom made necessary.
tours.how: A day across the city by metro, tram and bus. Ivrea is a separate day trip.

stops.note: The 1920s plant: cars built floor by floor going up, tested on the roof.
The 1961 Alweg monorail, closed in 1963.
Nervi and Ponti's hall for Italia '61, now a fenced ruin.
The 1937–39 plant, 2 million m²; Porta 5 was the gate of the labour struggles.
Mosso's 1957 church in Mirafiori.
1960s towers for the growing south-west.
Built in 1969–72 because the Monumentale was full.
Vitellozzi's arena built with the Fiat design office for Italia '61.
71 ha of 1958–68 public housing for 20,000 people.
Astengo's 1950s INA-Casa village.
Prefab slabs for southern migrants drawn by Fiat.

story: In the 1920s Fiat built Lingotto, then in 1937–39 Mirafiori. The company drew workers from the south and the city grew around them: Falchera, the Vallette, Corso Taranto.
The boom's showpiece was Italia '61: Nervi's Palazzo del Lavoro, Vitellozzi's arena and the monorail that ran for two years.

off.note: The other industrial dream: Olivetti's Ivrea.

tours.name: The years of lead
tours.intro: Riots, firebombs, a newspaperman shot in his doorway, the march that broke the Fiat strike, and the cinema fire that changed Italy's safety law.
tours.how: Centre stops on foot; Mirafiori by bus.

stops.note: 3 July 1969: the Corso Traiano riot by Gate 2. No plaque.
16 November 1977: the Red Brigades shot Carlo Casalegno in this doorway.
14 October 1980: the supervisors' march that ended the 35-day strike.
1 October 1977: a firebomb killed the student Roberto Crescenzio.
13 February 1983: 64 died behind chained exits.

story: From the Corso Traiano riot of 1969 to the Red Brigades' first murder of a journalist in 1977, Turin was at the centre of Italy's years of lead.
The period closed with the 'march of the 40,000' in 1980 and, in 1983, the Cinema Statuto fire.

tours.name: After Fiat: Olympics, ruins and reuse
tours.intro: When the factories closed, Turin reused some sites, staged the 2006 Olympics and left others to rot.
tours.how: City stops by metro, tram and bus; the Olympic sites are a mountain day by car.

stops.note: Renzo Piano's conversion; the track is now a garden.
The 2006 Olympic arch and footbridge.
The one not saved.
Nervi's hall restored as the central library, opening 11 Dec 2026.
Grandi Motori, being demolished since 2025.
The sunken rail corridor, Metro 2 from 2027.
The sneaker plant, abandoned 1998, becoming a culture hub.
Botta's church on the old steelworks, the chimney kept as a bell tower.
The December 2007 fire killed seven workers.

story: As industry left, its sites were reused: Lingotto, Parco Dora, soon the Trincerone. Others stand fenced: ThyssenKrupp, OGM, the Palazzo del Lavoro.
The 2006 Winter Olympics left an arch and an athletes' village in the city and two ruins in the mountains.

off.note: The 2006 bobsleigh track, funded for demolition.
The 2006 ski jumps, matting falling apart.

tours.name: Nervi, Vitellozzi and the great concrete halls
tours.intro: Nervi's two Turin halls, one reborn and one rotting, with Vitellozzi's arena and Fiat's factory.
tours.how: Along the river and Via Nizza by metro; the PalaRuffini is a bus ride west.

stops.note: Vitellozzi's own favourite, twin of his Rome Palazzetto.
The 1948–50 ferrocement vault, the 'cattedrale moderna'.
The concrete factory with a test track on the roof.
Sixteen concrete 'mushroom' columns under steel umbrellas.

story: Nervi roofed Salone B in 1948–50 and built the Palazzo del Lavoro with Ponti for 1961; Vitellozzi's PalaRuffini is the same year's other great roof.

tours.name: Mollino and the Neoliberty
tours.intro: Turin's own modernism: Mollino's opera house and offices, and the Neoliberty of Gabetti & Isola and Jaretti & Luzi.
tours.how: Centre stops on foot; Torri Pitagora by bus. Lago Nero is a mountain day.

stops.note: Mollino's largest work, inside Juvarra's façade.
Gabetti & Isola's early trading hall, closed since 1992.
Mollino's offices on a central core, with his helical stair.
Jaretti & Luzi's oyster-door provocation.
Jaretti & Luzi's forest of pillars.

story: Carlo Mollino left Turin the Teatro Regio and the Palazzo degli Affari; his sled station at Lago Nero is the mountain coda.
The Neoliberty generation answered rationalism with curves and craft: the Borsa, the Casa dell'Obelisco, Torri Pitagora.

tours.name: Concrete churches and a landscape cemetery
tours.intro: Post-conciliar Turin built churches in concrete for the new estates. Some are confirmed exposed concrete; the rest need your eyes.
tours.how: A transit day; Moriondo, Nichelino and Piossasco by car.

stops.note: Mosso's faceted concrete vault (1955–57).
The bell tower that dominates the skyline.
Bardelli's church with a gym in the undercroft.
A pointed 'cuspide' roof.
Bianco's all-concrete central plan with a floating roof.
Botta's towers and a steelworks chimney.
Hillocks hiding the concrete burial blocks.
Mosso's pentagon of six pillars, the Redentore's sibling.
Beams knitting into a net, modelled on the Redentore.
Roggero among the Mirafiori Sud estates.
A church made of factory-shed parts for Fiat Rivalta workers.

story: Under Cardinal Pellegrino (1965–77) the diocese built dozens of churches for the migrant estates. Mosso's Redentore set the type; Gabetti & Isola's Piossasco church is its most famous child.
Exposed concrete is confirmed for some, not all: the 'plausible' tags mark the ones to check in person.

tours.name: Industrial ruins and fenced giants
tours.intro: The fenced carcasses of industrial Turin, seen from the street.
tours.how: A bus day; everything is exterior only. Don't trespass.

stops.note: Nervi's abandoned hall.
Coachbuilding plant, abandoned 2001.
1911–52 asbestos factory.
The 2007 fire site.
Sneaker plant, abandoned 1998.
One chimney left.
The Ceres terminus, disused since 1986.
Grandi Motori's Basilica hall on a demolition site.
The overgrown rail trench.

story: Turin's industrial decline left giants behind; most are fenced, some are being demolished or converted. See them now.

tours.name: Nietzsche's last autumn, and the legends
tours.intro: Nietzsche lived here for four months and collapsed in the street on 3 January 1889. This tour keeps fact and legend apart.
tours.how: On foot in the old centre.

stops.note: His lodging: fourth floor, fifth window from the corner.
The ice-cream link is the least weak café claim.
A blog says he 'certainly' came; nothing supports it.
Piazza Carlo Alberto, where most sources place the horse story.
His name is on the wall, by tradition only.

story: Nietzsche lodged at Via Carlo Alberto 6 from September 1888, wrote Ecce Homo there and collapsed on 3 January 1889. The horse story is disputed; the café claims mostly legend.

tours.name: Writers' Turin: Rousseau to Primo Levi
tours.intro: Where writers lived, sat and died: Rousseau's abjuration, Pavese's café and hotel room, Primo Levi's house.
tours.how: On foot; Caffè Elena and Al Bicerin close on Wednesdays.

stops.note: Rousseau abjured Calvinism here in April 1728, aged 16.
Umberto Eco set a scene of The Prague Cemetery here.
A 1920s literary circle; the Gramsci line is marketing.
Pavese spent his time writing here; the Comune says so.
Pavese was found dead in room 346 on 27 August 1950.
Pavese, Einaudi and Ginzburg, per popular sources.
Primo Levi's birth and death house.

story: From Rousseau's months as a convert and footman to Pavese and Primo Levi, Turin's writers are easier to place than its philosophers.

tours.name: Gramsci and the red city
tours.intro: Gramsci's lodging and newspaper, the 1920 factory occupations, workers' clubs and the 1922 reprisal.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Fiat Corso Dante and Mirafiori by bus.

stops.note: L'Ordine Nuovo was written in these rooms.
December 1922: the squads burned the Camera del Lavoro.
The 1957 plaque: Gramsci lived at no. 15 in 1919–21.
A still-active workers' mutual-aid club.
Hub of the September 1920 occupations.
Porta 5, gate of the 1970s struggles.

story: Gramsci lived on Piazza Carlina in 1919–21 and wrote L'Ordine Nuovo, the paper of the factory councils that occupied Fiat in September 1920. The squads' reply came in December 1922.

tours.name: Science Turin: the meridian, nitroglycerine and Lombroso
tours.intro: Beccaria's measured baseline, Sobrero's lab, the old observatory, Lagrange, the induction motor, and the museums of anatomy and criminology.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then tram to the Valentino; Rivoli is a separate trip.

stops.note: The Turin end of the 1760 meridian baseline.
A noon line on the cathedral wall.
The city observatory, 1822–1912.
Beccaria taught physics here; the 1904 fire burned the manuscripts.
Nitroglycerine, first made in the lab here (1846–47).
The first real observatory was on this roof (1790).
An 18th-century pharmacy.
Lagrange's birthplace, 1736.
The natural-sciences museum, partly reopened.
The 1729 royal botanic garden.
Two centuries of Po floods, measured on a column.
Rolando's anatomy, Lombroso's criminology, Garnier Valletti's fruit.

story: Turin measured the Earth (Beccaria, 1760), made nitroglycerine (Sobrero, 1847) and the rotating magnetic field (Ferraris, 1885). Lombroso's museum shows science gone wrong, which is why it matters.

tours.name: Turin firsts: a parliament, a sandwich, a vermouth, an airmail
tours.intro: Things that started here, documented and disputed.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then tram and bus; Aeritalia is on Corso Francia.

story: Turin's claims range from documented (the parliament, Lavazza, Torino FC, the 1917 airmail) to tradition (vermouth, the tramezzino's exact year).

tours.how: On foot in the old centre.

story: Turin's small oddities sit close together, from Ferrero's bull to the smallest square. Most of the 'magic' stories attached to them are legend: see the myths tour.

tours.name: Magic Turin: legend against record
tours.intro: The 'black magic' city's favourite stops, each with what the record says.
tours.how: On foot from Piazza Statuto to Piazza Castello.

story: Guides sell Turin as a corner of a black-magic triangle. The stops are real; the stories mostly are not. Each note says which part is record.

tours.intro: Turin's odd infrastructure: the 1912 toll houses, baths that still sell showers, cast-stone urinals, ice-houses and a flood column.
tours.how: A bus day across the city; urinals are being demolished one by one.

story: The customs walls of 1853 and 1912 made the 'barrier' districts; the baths of the 1900s served workers' flats without bathrooms; the Renzi firm cast urinals sold across Italy. Several survive.

story: Turin's underground is mostly war: the 1706 mine war and the 1940s shelters. Four can be visited, by booking.

story: Turin's execution sites run from the French guillotine and the Savoy gallows to the 1864 massacre and the RSI firing squads.
